WITH driver_agg AS 
(
		WITH driver_stats AS 
		( 
		SELECT 
		ot.created,
		ot.order_id,
		ot.city_id,
		ot.driver_id,
		ot.price,
		ot.price_currency,
		ot.driver_company_id,
		fp.*
		FROM ng_public.company_order_try ot 
		JOIN admin_system.admin_system_city cy ON cy.id = ot.city_id
		JOIN 
				(
					WITH base AS (
						  SELECT
						    pp.id,
						    pp.client_id,
						    cl.external_id      AS fleet_id,
						    pp.amount,
						    pp.currency,
						    pp.created,
						    CASE WHEN pp."method" = 'regular' THEN date_trunc('week',pp.created) ELSE pp.created END AS time_locked,
						    pp.created_date,
						    pp."method"
						  FROM ng_payout.invoicing_payment_payout AS pp
						  JOIN ng_payout.invoicing_payment_client AS cl
						    ON pp.client_id = cl.id
						  WHERE pp.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('day', -180, current_date) AS date)
						    AND pp.state = 'finished'
						    AND pp."type" = 'ride_hailing_fleet'
						),
						prev_map AS (
						  SELECT
						    a.id                                   AS payout_id,
						    a."method",
						    MAX(b.created)                         AS prev_payout_created
						  FROM base a
						  LEFT JOIN base b
						    ON b.client_id = a.client_id
						   AND (b.created < a.created OR (b.created = a.created AND b.id < a.id))
						  GROUP BY a.id,a."method"
						)
						SELECT
						  b.fleet_id,
						  b.amount / r.rate                        AS payout_eur,
						  b.amount,
						  b.currency,
						  b.id,
						  b.created AS payout_created,
						  b.time_locked,
						  b."method",
						  p.prev_payout_created,
						  CASE WHEN p."method" = 'regular' THEN date_trunc('week',p.prev_payout_created) ELSE p.prev_payout_created END AS prev_time_locked
						FROM base b
						LEFT JOIN prev_map p
						  ON p.payout_id = b.id
						LEFT JOIN ng_public.currency_exchange_rates r
						  ON r.currency = b.currency
						 AND DATE(r.valid_on) = DATE(b.created)
						ORDER BY b.created DESC
					)
				AS fp ON fp.fleet_id = ot.driver_company_id 
						AND ot.created < fp.time_locked 
						AND CASE WHEN fp.prev_payout_created IS NULL THEN ot.created > (fp.time_locked - INTERVAL '7' DAY) ELSE ot.created > fp.prev_time_locked END
		WHERE ot.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('day', -188, current_date) AS date)
		AND ot.state = 'finished' 
		--AND ot.driver_company_id = 42499
		---
---- ////// ADD COUNTRY HERE ///// ---		
AND cy.country_code = 'ua'

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Hi [~accountid:712020:8c797c70-7a57-496e-aa3f-5d91df806eb2] , I’ve reviewed the TO DO list and have the following observations:

h3. *1. Claim filing (deadline: 29 Sept 2025)*

* There is no pre-determined format for the request to be submitted to the Galați Tribunal, but we can rely on the recommended template published [here|https://portal.just.ro/105/Documents/Ghid%20justitiabili%20-modele%20de%20cereri%20in%20materia%20insolventei%20final.pdf].
* *Mandatory elements:*
** Name of the creditor
** Domicile/registered office
** Amount owed
** Basis of the claim
** Supporting documentation
** Proof of payment of the 200 RON stamp fee
* I can draft the request quickly once I have all the necessary supporting documents from the relevant department.
* Since the request must be sent by post, it may take 20–30 calendar days (or longer) to reach the Tribunal registry.

h3. *2. Set-off considerations*

* Under *Art. 90 of the Insolvency Law*, set-off is expressly allowed both *before and after* the opening of insolvency proceedings:
“_(1) The opening of insolvency proceedings does not affect the right of any creditor to invoke the set-off of its claim against the debtor’s claim, provided that the conditions laid down by law for legal set-off are met on the date of the opening of the proceedings. The set-off may also be acknowledged by the judicial administrator or the liquidator._
_(2) The provisions of paragraph (1) shall apply accordingly to reciprocal claims arising_ *_after the date of the opening of insolvency proceedings_*.”
* Therefore, we can maintain the Agreement with the Debtor without losing the right to receive the Agency Fee, for which we have (i) a contractual basis and (ii) no legal impediment against the set-off.
* *However*, if the judicial administrator does not accept the set-off with our Agency Fee, which appears improbable, we cannot terminate the Agreement solely on insolvency grounds. In that scenario, we would either need another contractual reason for unilateral termination or pursue termination by mutual consent.

h3. *3. Next steps*

# Obtain supporting documents for our claim.
# Prepare and sign the request.
# Pay the 200 RON stamp fee.
# Send the request in *two original copies* to the Galați Tribunal via post.
# Optionally, contact the judicial administrator to find out:
#* How many priority creditors are ahead of us.
#* What the realistic chances are of recovering our receivable.

h3. *4. Guidelines*

* Yes, we will prepare draft templates and internal guidelines for future cases of this type.

{noformat}WITH unique_details AS
(
	SELECT 
	ca.country,
	pc.external_id AS fleet_id,
	CONCAT('https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet-company/companies/edit/', CAST(pc.external_id AS varchar)) AS link_to_v2_fleet,
	ca.client_id,
	ca.account_iban,
	ca.account_recipient,
	ca.account_swift,
	CASE WHEN TRUE THEN 1 END AS count_unique_case,
	max(ca.created) AS last_change_time
	FROM ng_payout.invoicing_payment_client_account ca
	JOIN ng_payout.invoicing_payment_client AS pc ON ca.client_id = pc.id
	WHERE pc.TYPE = 'ride_hailing_fleet'
	AND ca.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -1, current_date) AS date)
	AND ca.country = 'tw'
--	AND ca.client_id = 39643011
	GROUP BY 1,2,3,4,5,6,7
)
SELECT 
	x.fleet_id,
	x.link_to_v2_fleet,
	x.country,
	x.client_id,
	date_diff('day',max(x.last_change_time),now()) AS days_since_latest_change,
	sum(x.count_unique_case) AS count_cases,
	CASE WHEN sum(x.count_unique_case) BETWEEN 2 AND 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS notify_med_risk,
	CASE WHEN sum(x.count_unique_case) >= 4 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS notify_high_risk
FROM unique_details x
GROUP BY 1,2,3,4
HAVING sum(x.count_unique_case) > 1{noformat}

Hi [~accountid:626c24971a4eb30069d28197] [~accountid:6012ab10dc29b4006a594649] [~accountid:712020:bc7bca9c-4d13-42b6-9684-04014a47f7aa] as informed over Slack -  please find below a *legal review of all tender documents*. Please note that these documents contain extensive operational, vehicle, and driver requirements etc spread over 120+ pages (!), so this is not intended to be an exhaustive list of every obligation that must be observed but an overview of identified key risks (from my perspective). 

I also understand that [~accountid:712020:c0f6fbe7-f5ae-44e2-bb6c-8e5815ace0d9] has carried out a separate review from the B2G/Ops perspective and has already shared her comments in meetings with the business. That said, it is important to emphasize that the Ops team must be familiar with the requirements set out in this tender (as with any tender we may participate in going forward) to ensure we can actually meet these/have a plan for how to meet these. Also note that there are nuances in relation to the different municipalities under the tender. 

+Key risks include+:

* *Reclassification*: High risk of drivers being treated as employees due to prescriptive requirements, such as grooming standards, ID/uniforms, language proficiency, continuous training, regular and substitute driver obligations tie individuals to fixed citizens and routes etc;
* *Liability*: Unlimited liability, incl. subcontractors & consortia, with no cap;
Robust insurance should be put in place, business to discuss ways going forward with @daniel.severin.
* *Financial exposure*: Heavy penalties for e.g. service failures & emission compliance, including an annual cap of 5% of turnover of the framework;
* *Child transport obligations*: Child safety & driver vetting/training obligations, obtaining child/criminal records as well as certain driver training required for this purpose + overall higher safety risks when a tender includes transportation of children. 
** Handling children's data is deemed as highly sensitive - [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] to comment further and to assess how this is handled in practice.
* *Labour law*: Collective agreement compliance with severe sanctions.
** In my experience, this is something that media usually picks up on - asking a lot of questions in relation to how we, that do not employ drivers, can ensure such - therefore a plan how to handle this must be prepared (@elisabeth.gunnarsson has done such for Sweden). 

* In order to mitigate the risks, I recommend:
** Robust subcontractor agreements (post win) - similar to what's been done in Sweden - including back-to-back protection and other requirements coming from the tender;
** Ensure stronge insurance cover (given consortia, uncapped liability etc); and
** Ops/tender teams must be closely aligned with the requirements of the tender to ensure compliance (and minimize risk for penalties etc).

The full legal review can be found here: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1kpbXK1L4F6YYoDmxmhRfGIe241jnpcut/edit|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1kpbXK1L4F6YYoDmxmhRfGIe241jnpcut/edit|smart-link]

Please don’t hesitate to reach out if you have questions or if I can provide further support.

Request summary:

* *Objective*: Introduce direct call centre support as an exclusive benefit for Diamond Tier drivers, since they identified this as one of the most valued perks.
* *How it works*:
** Bolt compiles a list of Diamond Tier drivers along with links to their admin profiles.
** Only these drivers’ phone numbers are approved to reach the dedicated call line.
** When a driver calls, the system recognises the number, and the agent sees both the number and a shortened link to the driver’s profile.
** Clicking the link lets the agent verify the driver immediately, avoiding time-consuming searches in the admin panel.
* *Data handling & safeguards*:
** *Access control*: Only Smartly employees (Bolt’s call centre operators) can open the profile links, as they require Bolt-issued certificates.
** *Geonet’s role*: Geonet (the partner managing the call services) does not see or access driver data. They only receive anonymised, shortened links (e.g. [bit.ly/…|http://bit.ly/…]).
** *No personal data exposure*: Geonet cannot identify the driver, the panel name (“admin”) is hidden, and no IDs or personal codes are shared.
** *Privacy advantage*: This approach avoids giving Geonet direct access to sensitive identifiers, which would otherwise be required for them to handle calls.
* *Benefits*:
** *Exclusivity*: Only Diamond Tier drivers can use the benefit.
** *Efficiency*: Faster driver verification and shorter call handling times.
** *Security*: No disclosure of internal system details or driver personal data.
** *Compliance*: Sharing anonymised links is positioned as more privacy-preserving than providing raw identifiers.
* *Contractual setup*:
** This is part of the ongoing service agreement with Geonet (renewal, not a new agreement).
** No direct financial transaction attached — it is positioned as a service improvement rather than a commercial deal.
** Agreement is indefinite in duration.

👉 The project is framed as an *operational efficiency and driver loyalty initiative*, while also presenting itself as privacy-conscious by avoiding direct data transfers.

I looked at the Bangkok case we discussed on Monday: only few data points were available for Bangkok for demand uplifts.
*The issue is indeed related to bundles campaign* setup that is used in Bangkok.*What is bundles and what’s a difference with previously considered targeted campaigns?*
Bundle is a way to group the campaigns that is created to simplify setups for GAs. Eventually, instead of having test_id and several targeted campaigns under it, we have test_id with bundles that have several targeted campaigns.*Example of bundle setup* is [here|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/campaign-targeting/tests/rides_and_rental/3815012]: test with a [bundle|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/campaign-bundles/bundles/demand/145687], that has 3 rider targeted campaigns.
*Example of usual* [*test*|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/campaign-targeting/tests/rides_and_rental/3963989]: test with 1 targeted [campaign|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/campaign/targetedCampaigns/edit/1806271].From data point of view, uplifts from tests with bundles vs tests with campaigns do not look very different. And for the cases like Bangkok, is a an absolute improvement (see several cities that I plotted [here|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/1446731607677512?o=3829506390716583] and some are below too). *Hence, imposing a condition on having targeted campaigns and bundles should not make the cities with few bundles worse, and we gain a lot from having bundles in cities like Bangkok.* [*PR is here*|https://github.com/bolteu/data-science-databricks/pull/537]*.*

Hey [~accountid:6045db9a2b3f9a006a1ed804] -

How can we help you?

On August 15, Jeremy reached out saying that he had a conversation with Jevgeni B. and he had some valid points for improvement of the merchant profit pool analysis ([slack post|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C09ACE2AZEF/p1755248600602019])

Jevgeni adjusted the profit pool:

* Segmented orders per promotion type (+initial assumptions of the portion of demand):
** Orders w/o discounts or free delivery (10%)
** Orders with free delivery only (15%)
** Orders with discounts only (25%)
** Orders with free delivery and discounts only (50%)
* Calculated merchants' costs based on this distribution
* Calculated weighted average of the gross profit based on that distribution

I had a sync with Jevgeni on Aug 21 to discuss. We agreed that this way of looking at it is better. He also had his concerns, and his feedback are:

* Current SMB commissions (33%) leave SMBs with little to no profit, especially in Estonia, where he is familiar with the restaurant business;
* This way, we push SMBs too much, which makes it hard for them to gain value from the platform, pushing them to churn.
* We don’t focus enough on bigger accounts that can add more value when negotiated.

We agreed that many of the concerns are actually based on the way we operate Bolt Food - in isolation, our commission targets don’t shrink (too much) or push merchant to negative profit if merchants aren’t financing campaigns actively. When they do, they shrink their profitability. Even though we can look at it from a perspective of those campaigns are marketing expenses for the merchants, and are totally optional, the fact is that Bolt Food is a campaign-heavy platform and it is hard to gain significant traction if merchants (or us) don’t run campaigns. Therefore, we need to consider the merchant campaign costs as essential for the profit pool calculations.

We agreed that as I develop the V2 further, I’ll check in and get his feedback/ inputs.

To help them prioritise more effectively and solve the “everything is a high-risk problem”, I can propose adding {{Likelihood of being audited / fined / taken to court}}, which would act as a supplementary score in addition to the risk score. 

It would not replace or alter the existing logic, but would add an extra layer to prioritisation by helping us assess the likelihood of impact, which is then: _How likely are we to be audited and fined?_ _Have we already been fined and are we due for an already planned audit?_

*Impact of risk event 5:*

* >1% Impact to GMV, GDPR fine + regulatory, reputational consequences when non-compliance gets exposed

*Risk Score: 25*
{{Likelihood of being audited / fined / taken to court:}} Using existing Likelihood scale (1–5), with input from PP team on regulator history (audits, fines, investigations in this market/region or similar), and highlight this in the comments column.

Hey Daryl. 

Thanks for raising this topic with us. 

There are a few issues with the approach of only looking at canceled and finished order counts. A cancellation by it’s own isn’t necessarily harmful to Bolt. For example, if a cancellation fits any of the following scenarios, there’s no harm to our drivers: 

* cancellation happens when there’s not even a driver assigned to the order;
* happens when it’s back-to-back and the driver still has the previous order active;
* happens seconds after driver acceptance;
* and so on.

Another important issue is the time period you look at. A user might have a high count of cancellations in a certain week or month, but thousands of GMV within Bolt in a larger period. We wouldn’t want to hard-block such users. 

The approach we take to fight fake orders is to look at the ones that cause the most harm to us, meaning:

* they have a cost through a driver ticket (each CS ticket cost around 3 euros); 
* they have a cost through a cancellation fee compensation;
* they happen after a considerable part of the ETA was already driven by the driver, wasting the driver’s time.

I pulled some data for the 50 users you listed for the *past 4 months.*

!Screenshot 2025-08-26 at 13.21.40.png|width=2028,height=566,alt="Screenshot 2025-08-26 at 13.21.40.png"!

To start, got only 44 rows in the results. Means that there are already 6 users who didn’t even have any cancellations where a driver had accepted their request. 

Then we can explore some rows to illustrate what I’m talking about:

* user 263364544 (row 1)
** 624 cancellations in the last 4 months
*** only 28 were long cancels
** average wasted time from driver pretty low at 1.3 minutes per cancellation. 
** 10 driver tickets, 1.61 euros compensated in cancellation fees.
** 21.34 euros in GMV in the last 1 year
** I’m honestly not sure if this is a bad user. Avg time to cancel is so low, that it doesn’t seem the user is trying to waste time from our drivers. 
* user 276909449 (row 27)
** 30 cancellations, 22 long
** 16 euros GMV in 1y
** 367 minutes wasted from driver. avg over 12min per order.
** this is a clear one. that user is here to cause harm. we need to hard block those guys.
* user 240003332 (row 6)
** 112 cancellations, 4 long
** 1.1k euros in GMV in the last 1y
** this user was showing in your sheet with 0 finished orders. you could think it’s a bad user, but it produced more than 1k in GMV to Bolt. we shouldn’t act on these accounts.

I could keep going, but no need to do a deep dive on this specific list of users. I’ll run data for MY as a whole and will come up with thresholds where we’ll do progressive blocks based on the count of long cancellations a user has in a one-month period. It should help act on the worst offenders such as user 276909449 that would definitely get automatically hard-blocked by our system. 

I’ll get back to you later in the day with an update.

*Nurhidayat Thalib*  [9:00 AM|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C08P7S7M78T/p1755586814729059]
*Drive Verification Flow Revamp*
Hi everyone! Happy to announce that we're rolling out the new *Verification Flow Revamp* for Bolt Drive to *Employees*

*Problem*
Verification has been one of the main friction points impeding Bolt Drive's growth:

* Only *40% of users* who open the verification SDK complete the process in Free-Floating, and just *11%* in Station-Based car-sharing
* Another *22% of users drop* between DL and ID verification, often because they don’t have documents at hand, or flows feel too fragmented
* Overall, *verification issues make up 11% of all support tickets*, costing *0.32% of GMV*

The result: a painful user experience, unnecessary CS overhead, and lost conversion.*Solution*
We’ve redesigned the experience into a *single, streamlined flow* with better communication and clearer feedback:

* *Unified process*: Driving Licence, ID, and selfie checks are now handled in one continuous flow.
* *Clearer onboarding*: We highlight benefits upfront and explain what’s required.
* *Smarter error handling*: Users now see _why_ their verification failed and what to do next.
* *Progress indicators*: Riders always know where they're in the process.
* *Improved Lifecycle Comms:* To encourage users to complete their verifications.
* *Summary screen*: After finishing, users get a clear status view of each step.

This means a faster, less confusing experience for riders and fewer repeat support tickets.*Success metrics*
We expect a *+2.4% GMV uplift* and a measurable improvement in verification completion rates starting Q3 2025.*Rollout*

* We've rolled out to Employees since 18/08 16:00 (Yesterday).

*** {{CA.173.0}}

*Next steps*
While this revamp is a big UX leap forward, the following items will come in a later phase:

* Phone number verification
* Home address
* Tax ID (For applicable countries)

Hey [~accountid:5ce7b2073f4d610fdf029c16], thanks for the detailed explanation. I’m aligned with your points and I don’t have access to the same level of data to draw conclusions on my side.

The reason I raised this is because we’re receiving increasing complaints from drivers about repeated cancellations from the same rider/riders in general. For example:

* A rider books, the driver accepts, then the rider cancels.
* Shortly after, the same rider request comes in again, the driver accepts, and the rider cancels once more.
* In some cases, the driver even makes a U-turn to reach the rider shortly after they accepted, only for the trip to be cancelled.

This creates unnecessary inefficiencies for drivers—especially in city centers where traffic is heavy and roads are complex. It wastes their time in ways that aren’t fully captured in the system.

For cash orders, the issue is more pronounced since there’s no compensation if the driver has already driven some distance and rider cancel on them. And this will def not be reflected in cancellation fee, but perhaps using conditions like _ETA to rider >3 min + cash order_ could help approximate the impact.

Please let me know if you need any further info to define the threshold 🙏  Million thanks!

*In summary:*

* An employee/worker of ours has rented a vehicle from Avis and damaged it.
* Avis is asking us to pay the damages as they say the driver drove recklessly, which is a breach of their T&Cs and therefore invalidates or voids any of their insurances.
* We/Bolt have no insurance against this type of incident. We have Public Liability which covers damages caused by an employee or someone acting on our behalf but it excludes Motor Vehicles. 
* Communication was sent to Avis saying we do not agree to paying the damages since the driver had paid for their insurance from Avis, and we do not believe that they acted recklessly. 
* Avis has seemed to ignore this [letter|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1WixY5WiWZfTs6muTl-qADU5TXmcklmoy7iuJCcpaxXI/edit?usp=sharing]/email and continued to pursue us for the damages. 

From the insurance team's standpoint, we at Bolt have no insurance coverage for this incident. So, I can’t support the claim and have these damages reimbursed or paid for. 

Therefore, I see us having a few options:



# We pay the damages, and this is treated as an operational cost or loss to the business. 
# We continue to challenge this with Avis, and we go back to the points raised in the [letter|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1WixY5WiWZfTs6muTl-qADU5TXmcklmoy7iuJCcpaxXI/edit?tab=t.0], which they seemed to have ignored. However, I am not legal counsel; so, I am happy to support or share my view, but I think any communication should be conducted through legal channels.
# We engage with Avis and work out a settlement whereby we can cover some of the cost, but not all of them. However, this would need to be treated as an operational cost or loss, as there is no insurance in force here.

Both campaigns are risky. Bolt may face with *cease and desist letter*, *claim for reputational damages, claim about breach of right to privacy* (the latter needs to be evaluated locally) from the Swedish Royal family. These damages may be far above the budget of this campaign (x100). Please be aware that the fact we haven’t received any claims with Angela Merkel campaign is a matter of luck. 

Using Queen’s personality creates impression that Royal family approves/ endorses using Bolt’s products and services. 

*If Marketing decides to proceed with campaign consider the following*

* No logos, pictures, mentionings of the Royal family, no real names, symbols  of the Royal family on the crown, clothes. 
* Use neutral name  instead of real name of the Queen 
* No impersonalisation of moves specific to the person (e.g. gestures) - specific for German law but I advise to stick to this for other markets, as well 
* Scripts should be reviewed by Legal 

*Germany* *case law* 

There is extensive case law regarding the use of celebrity images (or of their lookalikes) in advertising.

*I.* The Regional Court of Cologne has ruled that advertising with a *Jogi Löw* (former coach of the German national football team) *lookalike* violates the general right of personality and the right to his own image
“The degree of similarity between the two persons and thus the differences in the external appearance of the two persons and with regard to their language habits for example, (…), are irrelevant in the end, because it is precisely a matter of making the plaintiff’s advertising value fruitful by attracting attention to the goods offered by the defendant. For this purpose, *_it is sufficient if a similarity between the two persons, given at first glance, creates the - albeit possibly only fleeting - idea that the person shown is the prominent applicant._*” (Regional Court of Cologne, decision of 01.06.2021, 28 O 218/21).

*II.*  In another case, the Higher Regional Court of Cologne has ruled on an advertising video of a furniture store using images of a *TV host lookalike*. The commercials showed scenes from a television quiz show in which a double played a host, which the court classified as a violation of the right to one’s own image. The court stated that in the case of advertising with predominantly commercial interests, the general right of personality of the person depicted without his consent is usually affected. “*This is because it is an essential part of the general right of personality to decide for oneself whether and in what way one’s own image should be made available for advertising purposes.* However, the focus is on the fact that the use of an image exploits the image or advertising value of the person depicted and gives the impression that the person depicted identifies with the advertised product, recommends it or praises it.” (OLG Cologne, judgement of 6 March 2014 - 15 U 133/13).

*III*. The *famous Sixt advertisement* which also made use of images of politicians is only comparable to a limited extent, as it was a *satirical examination of a political event of the time – the resignation of the former Minister of Finance*. In this case, *freedom of opinion prevailed the personal rights of the politician*. There is not such satirical component or allusion to a political event in the videos at issue. For the same reason, the videos are not likely to be entitled to protection under artistic freedom.

Data on queue movements doesn’t live in Looker yet, so a solution there is not possible at the moment. We can potentially do a custom query for you and export into a spreadsheet, but first we need to align on the goal and current state of things. 

----

Imo the issue lies in the fact that we forecast distinct (unique) cases based on their initial queue. So in scenarios that you described GTQ/GEQ would get the a higher allocation of full unique cases than in reality (in reality 20% of those cases could be handled in GTQ/GEQ only 10-20% of the time and the rest is spend in Local queue). In order to solve this, we should potentially start to forecast partial case counts, not distinct cases. Example: 

* Case comes in Q1, then goes to Q2 and finally Q3. 10% of handling time is spent in Q1, 50% in Q2 and 40% in Q3. When looking at actuals or feeding actuals to the forecasting system, we should consider:
** 0.1 of a case in Q1, 0.5 in Q2 and 0.4 in Q3. This will ensure that staffing will be correct. 

Do you agree with this or have any questions? 

----

Next step: today at 3:30 EEST CS OPS are having a call to discuss this topic, as similar concern was raised by Lukasz regarding Safety queues. During the call an agreement will be made on how to proceed further with this. If everyone is align, our team along with analytics engineering will work to refine how we look at actuals and how we feed data to forecasting for data science. At that point we can start exporting data on return rates as well. 

----

At the same time, we have some datasets available to look at initial vs final queue of cases. This is currently used to look at actuals vs forecast when measuring accuracy of data science forecasts.

Field: {{Support Case Tier Changed}} only has Event Created / Partition Event Created dimensions available. This means, Looker will capture support cases *created* in the last 8 weeks, regardless of when they were resolved. There doesn't seem to be any datapoints that would capture number of escalated tickets to CSPC that were closed in a particular week and what their First Touch was. As a side note, the First Touch looker metric was implemented specifically for the CS Privacy Team by Larisse as it was not possible to measure how long it takes them to action an escalated case. Why? Because tickets are all created in Tier 1/Tier 2 queue and also resolved there most of the time. CSPC queue is only used for the purposes of escalating the ticket and getting approval. Once approval is given, the ticket is sent back to Tier 1/Tier 2.

[~accountid:712020:726e5ea0-027c-4c31-a0fd-2c23b80dc56c]and  [~accountid:62615f256cb53d006a6a3fe1] see below:

Vouchers issued by Bolt cannot be treated as discount. In PY we have only intermediary B2B model which means that ride is provided by the driver, while the voucher is issued by Bolt.

* Passenger pays *reduced price* (fare – coupon value).
* Driver is entitled to the *full fare*, and the platform transfers to the driver:
** Fare – platform commission.
* The *coupon value is paid by the business customer* 

According to SET (Subsecretaría de Estado de Tributación) rules and *Decree No. 1030/13 (IVA)*:

* *Discounts granted must be shown directly in the invoice*.
* BUT here, the “coupon” is *not a discount borne by the driver* (since the driver still gets full fare).

That means:

* The *trip invoice should reflect the full trip price* (the “real value of the operation” from driver to passenger).
* The coupon is not a discount on that invoice, but rather an *additional billing line between the platform and the corporate client*.

In PY exists method of payment “voucher” - vale under the payment method 9 [https://docs.factpy.com/tablas/|https://docs.factpy.com/tablas/|smart-link] 

AFAIK, in Paraguay there is no equivalent classification of vouchers into SPV/MPV in the VAT law. Therefore my assumption would be as follow:

* *Step 1 – Business customer buys vouchers from Bolt*
** In Paraguay, this transaction is generally *not subject to VAT* if the voucher is just a _payment instrument_ - assumption 1.
** The sale of the voucher itself does not represent a taxable supply, because no service has yet been rendered -assumption 2
* *Step 2 – Vouchers are redeemed by users* 
** The *trip invoice* must be issued *at the moment of the ride (redemption)*.
** The VAT is due on the *full trip price*, regardless of whether the trip is paid by voucher, card, or cash.
* *Step 3 – Settlement between platform and driver*
** The driver’s income is the *full trip fare minus commission*, and VAT is calculated on the gross trip fare (driver → passenger).
** The platform invoices commission to the driver as usual.
** Let me know if it makes sense for you. If yes, maybe it could serve as starting point for your analysis.

h3. Why my cohort report numbers don’t match raw totals

# *Different purpose*
#* Raw totals = all rides in a quarter.
#* Cohort report = rides grouped by the quarter when users took their *first ride*.
# *Cohort logic*
#* Example: If a user’s first ride was in Q1 2018 → they belong to the *Q1 2018 cohort*.
#* Their later rides in Q2, Q3, Q4 still show under the *Q1 2018 row*, not under new rows.
# *What this means*
#* Raw totals for Q1 2018 include:
#** New Q1 users’ rides
#** Old users (from 2017 or before) still riding in Q1.
#* Cohort report for Q1 2018 only includes:
#** Rides from *new users who started in Q1 2018*.
# *Extra filters* (in cohort script)
#* Excludes test/bot/blocked users.
#* Only allows certain countries.
#* Drops rides before each country’s “launch” quarter.
#* Requires user’s home country = ride’s country.

*Simple takeaway:*
The raw totals count *everyone’s rides* each quarter.
The cohort report counts rides *only from users who first joined in that quarter* (plus their later activity).
That’s why the numbers are smaller and don’t match.

Hey [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a], coming back to you. The simple answer is that we would rather avoid testing this feature in consent-based markets. The reason is that, unlike in the EU where we can justify the activity on the basis of legitimate interest (as you correctly pointed out), these markets do not allow for that legal ground. Instead, our Passenger Privacy Notices there cover all processing activities under a general consent framework, which is not an ideal legal position, but has been our approach to date. By that logic, any activity described in the PN could be treated as acceptable.

However, at present, the PN in consent-based markets does not mention the use of “device data” for personalised ride suggestions or profiling (or similar activities). As such, the current framework does not clearly extend to the Comfort Rides profiling use case. Rolling out tests in those markets without updating the PN would therefore create unnecessary risk, since passengers would not have provided valid consent for this specific processing.

In practical terms, I would still consider the risk profile *low* (non-sensitive data, limited user impact, unlikely to trigger regulatory action), but it could be flagged if challenged. 

*Moving Forward:*

Inspired by that case, we are planning to update the Privacy Notices accordingly to cover the Device Data in such processing activities. If completed, we would be fine with the roll-out in those markets as well.

On the countries below, since TH has a LI basis, my approach would be similar to yours, as in cases of the EU. In regards to AZ, I would not recommend that.

Hey Daryl.

I’ve updated the rules. We’ll progressively block users based on their count of long cancels in the last running month.

* 0-10 GMV
** 1m aggregates
*** long_cancels >= 3: 1hr block
*** long_cancels >= 5: 1 day block
*** long_cancels >= 7: 1 week block
*** long_cancels >= 8: hard-block

* 10-50 GMV
** 1m aggregates
*** long_cancels >= 7: 1hr block
*** long_cancels >= 9: 1 day block
*** long_cancels >= 10: 1 week block
*** long_cancels >= 12: hard-block

Based on June’s data, the monthly impact caused by users that hit above thresholds is:

* 222 users
* 114 are considered bad users, where the cost that they generated to us in a month is at least 3 times more than the profit we got from the GMV they've produced in the last 1 year
** 61% ratio
* 1.3k cancelled orders
* 656 long cancels, where long is when the cancellation happens at least 2 minutes after driver acceptance and at least half of the pickup ETA has passed. for example, for an ETA of 6 min, cancellation happens at least 3 min after driver acceptance.
* 276 euros in cost to us
** 252 CS tickets
** 24 euros compensated to drivers for cancellation fees
* 132 hours wasted from drivers
* 2.4k euros GMV produced by these users in the last 1y running period
Rules should help reduce a bit the escalations from drivers, but won’t solve the problem completely. We’re still reacting after harm is done. At least we’ll cap the harm that each user will cause.

Hi [~accountid:712020:548c71a6-d1f4-404d-9c5e-482bc0de371a] – jumping in here as I was also part of the Angela Merkel campaign in Germany.

*Appreciate the thorough reply!* To clarify, are we basically saying that the legal assessment made around Angela Merkel a year ago was incorrect (since it was green-lighted by Legal), or has something changed since in how these cases are interpreted? My understanding back then was that the rationale for approval was based on:



# The character is an imitation/parody, without direct reference by name, title, or role.
# It is left to the viewer’s interpretation, rather than explicitly stating who is being portrayed.
# The person being portrayed should not commercially monetize on their name or brand (unlike, for example, athletes or musicians who build their business around their persona, using it as intellectual property, and/or monetize on their likeness).

This case is arguably even less sensitive than Angela Merkel, since Silvia is not a political figure — and, like Angela, also not someone who monetizes her likeness the way athletes , musicians or celebrities do (e.g., Taylor Swift, Roger Federer, Kim Kardashian etc.).

That said, above court cases are all very interesting as even a “fleeting similarity” or “recognizable likeness” that makes people think of the actual person seems to be enough for a verdict. *But maybe with an important difference:* all of those individuals had built their names in a way where their reputation is directly tied to their monetization. I’d argue that politicians and royals are a bit different, since (1) politicians choose the spotlight but don’t directly monetize their likeness, and (2) royals also don’t monetize their likeness. I suppose that’s also why companies like IKEA had the guts to launch something similar in Germany around Angela Merkel (see image below). 

It’s also worth noting that parody of the Swedish royal family is already established in Swedish culture and media, given their quite unique way of presenting themselves and how they speak. For example, the TV show _Hey Baberiba_ ran on national TV and openly using Silvia’s name and making it very clear who they were portraying (though this was 20 years ago). By comparison, our interpretation would be more subtle.

*With that in mind from a legal and reputational perspective, shouldn’t that make this case even less risky compared to Merkel, or would you still advise going another route?*

_P.S. - I’d say the idea works either way — we can still pursue a generic royalty character without adding Silvia’s accent or resemblance, though of course that removes a lot of the edge and virality potential. The greatest marketing is often what stirs things up, carefully provokes, and sits on the edge. That said, I obviously wouldn’t want us to get sued, but I find it fairly unlikely that someone from the royal administration would spend time going after a company for simply resembling an older royal woman with an accent._

Answer: 
*I read the advice provided from 2 birds in this way:*

* The Serviceattest and related declarations do *not* need to be uploaded or submitted with our tender bid.
* The contracting authority will request them later in the process (before contract award) and set a deadline for submission.
* Even though it’s not required for the bid, the law firm recommends *starting the process early*. This is because:
** Authorities may take up to two weeks to process the request.
** Foreign board members in particular must provide additional documents (consent form, solemn declaration, passport copy, etc.).
* The sentence you highlighted (“_Therefore, the necessary declarations are actually already available on the website and can be applied relatively easily_”) is simply clarifying that:
** The process of obtaining the Serviceattest is straightforward.
** Danish board members get their consent forms automatically.
** Foreign members just need to submit the extra materials.
** This *does not mean* you need to download and submit them with the tender, as this is not a requirement (as ESPD suffices). It means the process is accessible and shouldn’t be a barrier once you start.

Indeed, the points discussed regarding this initiative remain valid.
Please see below for a more detailed assessment and risk mitigation plan we would suggest implementing to proceed safely:

----

+*Legal Risks*+

Distributing branded safety equipment like helmets -especially free of charge- could potentially be used as evidence of an employment-like relationship if not managed properly.

h4. +Mitigation Measures+

# *Do Not Provide Helmets for Free* 
#* Charge a symbolic price for the helmets, even if minimal (e.g., Gs. 10,000), to reinforce that this is not an employment benefit.
#* Alternatively, sell the helmets at cost through a third-party vendor or platform.
#* Ensure that participation is completely optional and not linked to any performance metrics or onboarding requirements.
# *Avoid Direct Provision by Bolt*
#* Ideally, route helmet sales through a third party - such as:
#** A local vendor
#** A logistics partner
#** An independent online store 
#* Bolt can then communicate availability of helmets, but not handle payment or delivery directly.
# *Avoid Use of Language Suggesting Obligation or Uniform*
#* Messaging should clarify that branded helmets are *optional promotional items*.
#* Do *not* refer to them as part of a “uniform” or “standardised equipment”.
# *Track Distribution*
#* Keep records of who purchases the helmets and how they were distributed to ensure transparency in case of audits or legal scrutiny.

----

Hello, [~accountid:712020:15ac5f93-eb38-4463-bfc9-9c893253e9de], thank you for the ticket. 
Since the agreement is of indefinite duration, Bolt may terminate it in accordance with Clause 8.3, i.e., where there is a sufficient ground to do so. The agreement does not define what constitutes “sufficient ground,” but if there has been a material change in the economic circumstances making it difficult to continue performing the agreement, Bolt could potentially rely on this as a basis for unilateral termination, should it wish to do so.

Clause 13.5 of the General T&C provides for unilateral possibility for Bolt to amend the General Terms, but this does not extend to amendments of the Special Terms. Therefore, unilateral amendments of the Special Terms by Bolt would not be permissible.

In this situation, I would recommend engaging with the restaurant to agree on termination of the current agreement and the conclusion of a new one, if the aim is to amend a part of the Special Terms.

If you have any other questions - please let me know, thanks 🙏

Hi [~accountid:712020:9c9d169e-9898-4461-8613-c311edb214ba] , The _Wait & Save_ feature allows riders to voluntarily wait for a lower fare, with no opt-out for drivers. Drivers receive these requests as part of the standard ride category, and fares are calculated using standard pricing logic.

* According to the Central Legal assessment, _Wait & Save_:
** *Does not require T&C updates* as it doesn't affect driver rights or obligations. Drivers remain under the standard category and are not required to qualify or accept special conditions.
** *Does not trigger a new contractual category* under EU P2B Regulation or Platform Work Directive (PWD). There is no opt-out necessary since this does not modify driver obligations or earnings.
** *Must not reduce driver earnings below standard levels*. If this occurred, it would create risk under Croatian consumer protection (Zakon o zaštiti potrošača) and labour reclassification principles.
** Drivers *retain full discretion* to *accept or reject* any incoming ride request, as per Bolt’s general Terms and Conditions (Art. 4.4 Driver T&Cs).
** Drivers are not *contractually required* to perform a Wait & Save ride if they choose not to — it’s just presented without a label.

 [~accountid:712020:7f47c2af-14e1-4206-a795-ac87cb906276] you are correct that this qualifies as high-risk processing under GDPR. However, this does not mean it is prohibited altogether. The key factor is how the setup will work in practice.

Before launch, we will need close alignment with product and local operations to ensure the data flows are clearly mapped and safeguards are embedded. Provided that we are transparent, rely on parental consent, and implement appropriate measures, there are no fundamental blockers from a privacy perspective.

One additional area of concern is safety. This goes beyond privacy but will need to be reviewed in parallel to confirm what protective features can be enabled.

|*Processing of personal identity codes*|The Finnish Data Protection Act allows processing of a personal identity code (the 11‑character ID number on Finnish passports/ID cards) only if the data subject consents or if it is necessary to uniquely identify the person to perform a statutory duty or to implement the rights and duties of the data subject or controller. The law lists examples where the personal identity code may be processed (credit granting, insurance, health‑care, employment, etc.) and prohibits unnecessarily entering the code into documents.|As ride‑hailing is not one of the listed activities, simply collecting and storing Finnish personal identity codes for convenience would exceed the statutory purpose. Bolt should therefore design the verification flow to confirm identity without storing or using the full personal identity code.|
|*Use of ID documents for identity verification*|The Data Protection Ombudsman notes that a personal identity code is “not intended for determining identity” and controllers “may not base their identification procedures solely” on the code; it may only be asked for alongside other information when necessary. In a 2023 DPA case, an online directory was fined for requiring a copy of a customer’s ID document when it had no legitimate reason to request it; the DPA stressed that a controller may request additional information to verify identity only when it has reasonable grounds to doubt identity and should not collect an ID copy without a clear need.|Bolt must demonstrate that collecting an ID document (and selfie) is necessary and proportionate to its legitimate interest in protecting women drivers. Simply copying and storing ID images would breach the Finnish data‑minimisation requirement if the same objective can be achieved with less intrusive means.|
|*Discrimination*|Finland’s Act on Equality between Women and Men prohibits direct or indirect gender‑based discrimination and states that treating someone differently on the basis of gender, pregnancy, gender identity or expression is unlawful. However, positive action to improve women’s safety and opportunities is permitted under EU gender‑equality law when proportionate and based on objective need.|Because the W4W category remains available to riders of all genders and aims to protect women drivers, the risk of gender discrimination is lower. Nevertheless, Bolt should be ready to justify the need for a women‑focused category as a positive measure to address documented harassment and safety issues.|
|*Other regulatory requirements*|Finnish taxi and ride‑hailing rules require a taximeter or other system to record identifying information of the entrepreneur, driver and vehicle, trip details, price and payment method, but they do not obligate providers to collect passenger identity documents.|There is no statutory requirement to collect passenger ID. Therefore, any collection must rely on GDPR‑compliant lawful bases (e.g., legitimate interest) and meet data‑protection principles.|

TfL expects to start receiving completed Information Sharing Agreements templates by 5 September 2025.

:green: *Scope of data sharing*: 

# *Fleet Data* (Every 4 weeks)
## Average number of e-bikes on-street per day (rounded)
## Maximum number of e-bikes on-street per day (rounded)
# *Demand Data* (Every 4 weeks and cumulatively)
## Total number of trips
## Total distance travelled
## Trips per borough
## Average trip duration and distance
# *Safety Data* (Every 4 weeks and cumulatively)
## Serious and fatal collision/casualty reports. Includes: time, date, location, conditions, vehicle/user details, whether reported to police, etc.
# *Ad Hoc Data*
## Trip-level geolocation data (in focused areas only). Shared only as pseudonymised and linked to a trip ID, *not* to a user ID.

This is the industry standard practise for transport authorities to request this data sharing from micromobility operators.

Hi [~accountid:620f8ddea715c600691514af] !

Thank you for raising this ticket.

Given the urgency of the request, we are providing a preliminary assessment based on currently available online information. 
If it is decided to move forward with the project, we recommend giving us time for a more in-depth review and consult with our external legal counsel, considering the specificities of the subject matter and the fact that the sale and delivery of medicines is a highly regulated activity in Portugal.


# +*Over-the-Counter Medicines (OTC/MNSRM - Medicamentos Não Sujeitos a Receita Médica)*+

*Online Sale & Home Delivery:*

* +Only pharmacies and MNSRM outlets that are registered with INFARMED+ may sell and deliver OTC medicines online or to the home, meaning Bolt would need to verify that partners are properly licensed. You can check the authorized places [here.|https://www.infarmed.pt/documents/15786/1559752/Listagem+de+locais+de+venda+de+medicamentos+n%C3%A3o+sujeitos+a+receita+m%C3%A9dica+%28LVMNSRM%29+que+dispensam+medicamentos+ao+domic%C3%ADlio+ou+atrav%C3%A9s+da+internet/79c47e06-2d38-47f5-b0e5-7ed684613f91]
* +Deliveries must be executed by appropriately qualified personnel (pharmacists or pharmacy technicians)+, supervising the dispensing. Home delivery must observe Good Distribution Practices (GDP) regarding packaging, temperature control, security, etc. 
+Article 2(2) of Portaria n.º 1427/2007+ states that: _“A entrega ao domicílio deve ser feita sob a supervisão de um farmacêutico, no caso de farmácia, ou de um farmacêutico ou técnico de farmácia, no caso de local de venda de medicamentos não sujeitos a receita médica.” (EN: Home delivery must be supervised by a pharmacist, in the case of a pharmacy, or by a pharmacist or pharmacy technician, in the case of a place selling medicines not subject to prescription_)_._ This means there is a legal requirement that a qualified professional (pharmacist or pharmacy technician) must supervise the home delivery—the act of delivery must occur under their supervision.
+Article 3(3) of Portaria n.º 1427/2007+ also states that: _“A entrega de medicamentos ao domicílio só pode ser assegurada pela farmácia ou, no caso de medicamento não sujeito a receita médica pelo local autorizado à respectiva venda, onde o medicamento é solicitado.” (EN: Home delivery of medicines can only be provided by the pharmacy or, in the case of non-prescription medicines, by the authorised point of sale where the medicine is requested._)
In practical terms, *this implies delivery must be handled directly by the pharmacy or licensed outlet—not by a third-party courier without supervision.*

In [INFARMED website|https://www.infarmed.pt/web/infarmed/perguntas-frequentes-area-transversal/medicamentos_internet] it is clearly stated that:
_”_*_Who can deliver medicines?_*
_The legislation states that “home delivery must be carried out under the supervision of a pharmacist, in the case of a pharmacy, or of a pharmacist or pharmacy technician, in the case of an OTC outlet.”_
_Home delivery of prescription medicines must comply with the rules for dispensing prescription medicines. Thus, the professionals performing home delivery must have the qualifications and training appropriate for dispensing prescription medicines._
_Home delivery of non-prescription medicines must also comply with the dispensing rules for non-prescription medicines, meaning that professionals authorized to dispense in OTC outlets must have appropriate training for dispensing medicines._

*_Can the pharmacy send medicines by mail or courier?_*
_No, the legislation requires that medicines must be delivered at home in compliance with the rules of supervision, qualification, and training appropriate for dispensing medicines, and in accordance with the transport rules set out in the Good Distribution Practices of Medicines._
_The Good Distribution Practices of Medicines establish:_
_“(...) 9.4 – Medicines must be transported throughout their circuit in such a way that:_
_a) Their identification is not lost;_
_b) They do not contaminate and are not contaminated by other products or materials;_
_c) Special precautions are taken against spillage, breakage, or theft;_
_d) They are kept in safe conditions and not exposed to inappropriate heat, cold, light, humidity, or other adverse factors, nor to the action of microorganisms or pests._
_9.5 – Medicines requiring temperature control during storage must also be transported under appropriate special conditions. (...)”_

+Other relevant information:+
* The geographical scope of delivery is limited to the municipality of the pharmacy and the neighboring municipalities.
* Websites must display the EU common logo, linking to the national register so consumers can verify authorization.
* Websites must show mandatory information: price, payment methods, delivery area, estimated delivery time, name of the technical director, and must maintain a record of orders (products, quantities, municipalities), available for INFARMED inspection.
* Sites must clearly and in advance publicize any fees associated with online dispensing and home delivery. Prices must align with those advertised.


       +Digital Advertising (OTC/MNSRM):+

* Deliberation No. 20/CD/2024, issued by INFARMED on 29 February 2024, sets forth the Good Practices for Advertising Over-the-Counter Medicines (OTC) through digital channels. It defines rules for digital advertising of OTC medicines. According to it, all digital advertisements must include:
- A *prominent rectangular blue banner* containing the warning:
_“Deve ler cuidadosamente todas as informações constantes da embalagem do medicamento e do seu folheto informativo e, no caso de dúvida ou de persistência dos sintomas, deve consultar o seu médico ou farmacêutico.”_
- Additionally, they must provide a *direct link* to the most up-to-date version of the *package leaflet (folheto informativo)*.

These provisions are central to ensuring that consumers receive accurate and responsibly presented information when encountering OTC medicine ads online.


# +*Prescription-Only Medicines (MSRM)*+

*Online Sale & Home Delivery:*

Online ordering of prescription medicines is permitted, but only if ALL the following conditions are met:

* +Authorized Establishment+ - Only licensed pharmacies registered with INFARMED for home delivery/online dispensing may provide this service. OTC outlets cannot sell prescription medicines.
* +Prescription Requirement+ - A valid prescription (receita médica) must be presented and verified before dispensing.
* +Supervision by Qualified Personnel+ - Dispensing and delivery must occur under the supervision of a pharmacist.
* Regarding home delivery, what was said above also applies here, which means +home delivery must be made by the pharmacy, not by an unqualified third-party courier.+
* +Delivery Conditions+: Medicines must be delivered only within the pharmacy’s municipality and adjacent municipalities; Must follow Good Distribution Practices (GDP): correct packaging, temperature control, product integrity, protection against contamination, spillage, theft, etc.
* +Website Requirements+ - Pharmacies must have a dedicated website with mandatory information: Price of dispensing & delivery services; payment methods; delivery area & estimated time; name of the responsible pharmacist; must display the EU common logo, linking to INFARMED’s national registry; 
* +Record-Keeping:+ Pharmacies must keep records of orders (products, quantities, municipalities) and make them available to INFARMED upon request.

* User A originally created the Bolt account and linked it to their phone number.
* Later, User A changed their phone number.
* The old number was recycled by the mobile operator and reassigned to User B (the reporting user).
* When User B logged in with that number, they were accidentally logged into User A’s account, since it was still linked to the old number.
* User A’s device still had an active session and, on 11 August, tried to use the account again (changed name, attempted to update number).
* We have now logged User A’s device out. User B is the only one with access going forward.

** *datapoints reduced* from 78 to 28. See the [illustrative template|https://finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/ba0d4713-d4b4-4668-acd3-4df31358d029_en?filename=250704-taxonomy-delegated-act-examples-template_en.pdf].
** *activities cumulatively accounting for <10%, capex or opex* *can be reported separately as non-material*
* The amendments face a four-month scrutiny period (extendable by two). If unchallenged, they take effect on 1 January 2026 and will cover the 2025 financial year. However, undertakings are given the option to apply the measures from 2026 if that's more convenient.

Thank you for raising this ticket.
We are going to provide you an overview of the Legal Framework in MT regarding the selling of medicines based on online information, having in consideration that you need this information in short time.

If it is decided to move forward with the project, we recommend giving us time for a more in-depth review and eventually consult with our external legal counsel, considering the specificities of the subject matter.


+*Medicines Act and Related Regulations*+

Medicines Act, Chapter 458 (and subsidiary legislation including S.L. 458.16) provide that:

* Pharmacies must hold a valid licence tied to specific premises, issued by the Licensing Authority (Supt. of Public Health) 
* Licence conditions cover dispensing, storage, premises standards, and the role of the managing pharmacist
* The Medicines Authority oversees product authorisations, inspections, safety, advertising, and supply chain compliance


+*Online Sales and Internet Pharmacies:*+

While Malta does not license standalone _internet pharmacies_, from the collected information it seems that licensed physical pharmacies can use digital platforms like Bolt to receive orders and coordinate delivery — provided that all obligations (prescription validation, pharmacist oversight, traceability) are fulfilled.


General information:

* Pharmacy licence must be verified: Bolt must only onboard pharmacies licensed by the Maltese Licensing Authority (via Medicines Authority).
* Pharmacist must retain control: All prescription validation and dispensing is done inside the pharmacy by a licensed pharmacist.
* Traceability: Pharmacist must be able to check himself the prescription (in case of prescription medicine) and must be able oversight of orders.
* No dispensing by Bolt: Bolt cannot select, prepare, or substitute medicines — its role is limited to platform facilitation + delivery.
* Advertising restrictions: Medicines advertising in Malta is regulated; Bolt must ensure no promotional practices breach the Medicines Act (especially for prescription-only medicines).
* Pharmacies may only supply medicines authorised in Malta and must dispense them according to Maltese classification (OTC vs Prescription)
* Consumers are warned against buying from unregulated or anonymous online sources due to risks of falsified or unsafe medicines.



+*Classification and Prescription Rules*+

Maltese law classifies products in line with Directive 2001/83/EC:

* Prescription-only medicines (POMs) require a valid medical prescription, are dispensed by a pharmacist, and must adhere to strict rules—including for psychotropic ("green") prescriptions which require control cards and are dispensable only once, with urgent exceptions allowing up to one-week supply
* OTC (Over‑the‑Counter) medicines can be dispensed without a prescription, but still must be dispensed by, or under the supervision of, a pharmacist at a licensed pharmacy


*A. OTC (Non-Prescription) Medicines*

+Definition:+ Medicines classified as not requiring a prescription under the Medicines Act (Cap. 458) and EU Directive 2001/83/EC.

+Sale rules:+
- Can be dispensed without a prescription.
- Must still be sold only through licensed pharmacies (not supermarkets or non-pharmacy retailers).

+Online/Distance selling:+
- Licensed pharmacies may sell OTC medicines through online channels or intermediary platforms (like Bolt), provided they comply with Medicines Authority rules.

+On Bolt side:+

* No prescription checks are required, but sale/dispense must still be supervised by a pharmacist. These medicines can be dispensed without a prescription, but they must still be sold only through licensed pharmacies (not supermarkets or non-pharmacy retailers). Therefore, Bolt would need to ensure listings originate only from Maltese licensed pharmacies (verify against Medicines Authority’s registry).
* Bolt would also need to ensure that products are clearly labeled as OTC.
* Platform would need to include disclaimers encouraging pharmacist consultation.
* Manage delivery per pharmacy instructions (e.g., temperature-sensitive items).


*B. Prescription Medicines*

+Definition:+ Medicines designated as prescription-only by the Medicines Authority.

+Sale rules:+ Can only be supplied upon presentation of a valid prescription signed by a doctor/dentist/nurse (as per Maltese law).

Dispensing must always be carried out by a pharmacist, who checks authenticity, dosage, and patient suitability.

+Special rules:+

* Antibiotics: prescriptions valid only for 10 days.
* Psychotropic/narcotic drugs (“green prescriptions”): stricter rules apply, including control cards and single dispensation.

+Online/Distance selling:+

Possible, but only if:

* The pharmacy verifies the prescription before dispensing - this must be ensured.
* Secure systems exist for patients to submit/upload prescriptions.
* The pharmacist confirms compliance before handing over to the courier.

+On Bolt side:+

* Allow pharmacies to receive and verify prescriptions in compliance with Maltese rules.
* Support upload of prescriptions (ensuring they meet legal criteria: legibility, prescriber details, date, dosage, patient details, etc.)—as per Medical Council guidance
* Integrate controls for: Expiry of prescriptions; Green prescriptions (ensure control card, single dispensation rule); Clearly indicate items requiring prescriptions.



+*Courier delivery of medicines seems to be legally allowed in Malta*++,+ provided all key conditions are respected:

- dispensing of medicines must be carried out by a licensed pharmacy, under the responsibility of a pharmacist;
- once a medicine has been dispensed by a pharmacist (i.e. checked against prescription, packaged, and labelled correctly), it may be delivered to the patient; 
- the law does not prohibit the use of third-party couriers for this delivery, as long as the dispensing obligations are already fulfilled by the pharmacy.

+Conditions for Lawful Courier Delivery+

* Dispensing responsibility stays with the pharmacy (as said above);
* Chain of custody & integrity - Medicines must be transported in conditions that maintain their safety, quality, and efficacy. These obligations flow from the Good Distribution Practice (GDP) principles adopted under the Medicines Act.
* Prescription medicines: the pharmacist must have validated the prescription before handover to the courier; Bolt’s role is limited to delivering a sealed, dispensed package from the pharmacy to the customer.
* Pharmacy remains liable: under Maltese law, the pharmacy and its pharmacist retain legal responsibility for ensuring the medicine reaches the correct patient in safe condition.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Data Sharing with OMV*
{panel}

Since we are sharing driver personal data with OMV (i.e., the OMV card numbers), it is generally advisable for Bolt to enter into a *data sharing agreement* with OMV to cover this - this is because a DSA ensures that Bolt is protected in case OMV’s non-compliance / data breaches result in any liability for Bolt.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Promoting OMV to Bolt drivers*
{panel}

Posting OMV to Bolt drivers via *blog posts / in-app stories* not directed at specific users does not raise any material direct marketing issues, and so I have {color:#36b37e}*no concerns from a privacy POV*{color} (/)

With regards to sending *push notifications* and *emails (newsletters)* to drivers about the OMV discounts, this is caught by direct marketing rules. As such, these notifications *should only be sent to drivers that have consented / opted-in to receiving them* (i.e., drivers that have consented to ‘partner offers’ on their account) (!)

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Contents of the form*
{panel}

If OMV *_insists_* on including the tickboxes (i.e., this is a +_deal-breaker_+ for them), then we can {color:#4c9aff}*take the following approach*{color}:

* *Change the opening text* to the following (instead of my previous suggestion, since we are now relying on consent instead), so that we have at least included a link to our privacy notice: “_By completing this form, you ensure that your data will be correctly processed and transferred to OMV Česká republika, s.r.o. This information is used to verify and link your OMV customer card to the bonus program so that you can take full advantage of all available discounts and benefits. For further information on how Bolt processes and shares your personal data,_ _please refer to our privacy notice available at_ [+_https://bolt.eu/cs-cz/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/?category=rides_+|https://bolt.eu/cs-cz/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/?category=rides]”.
* *Reinsert the checkboxes*, but *tweak the language* to the following:
** “_I agree to Bolt sharing my OMV card number with OMV Česká republika, s.r.o._”
** “_I agree to be included in the segmentation by OMV Česká republika, s.r.o. based on data about my purchasing behavior._”

Ultimately, the second checkbox is not really a concern for us anyway, so if OMV refuses to proceed unless these are included, then we can proceed on this basis.

(!)  However, if we take this approach, please {color:#ff5630}*make sure you have explained my position properly to OMV Legal*{color}. In particular:

* By asking in the form for the drivers to _consent_ to the sharing of their OMV card number, we must allow that driver to withdraw their consent at any time and for any reason. Hi [~accountid:712020:6cf755e4-2536-45f4-814b-7e7ef0cdbd97] !

Thanks for raising this – it’s an important point as courier engagement and reclassification risks need to be carefully balanced in Portugal.



+*Where our risk lies*+
The main legal risk is reclassification of couriers as employees. Portuguese courts have been increasingly sensitive to this, particularly in the food delivery space, and we’ve already seen precedents where factors such as control over couriers (instructions, mandatory shifts, monitoring, penalties, and training) were decisive for reclassification.

Any direct or prescriptive communication to couriers that could be interpreted as Bolt “managing” or “supervising” their work (e.g. telling them when, how or where to work, or disciplining them) increases exposure.


+*How big the risk is*+
In Portugal, the risk is very high compared to other EU markets because:

* The Labour Inspectorate and courts are active in pursuing reclassification in the sector.
* Independent couriers were phased out in April 2023, with fleets now supplying labour. Even so, aggressive comms to couriers can still be cited as evidence of hidden employment relationships.
* Litigation costs, potential back-pay of employment benefits, and reputational risks make this a top legal exposure for Delivery.



+*Market intelligence / what competitors are doing*+
We don’t have clear evidence that competitors in PT have completely frozen comms. However, we know competitors are losing some of the reclassification cases in Portugal that they are part of, while Bolt has so far avoided such outcomes. This reinforces that our more conservative strategy has been paying off from a litigation-risk perspective.


+*Sensitivity to business impact*+
We are very conscious that this cautious approach restricts some commercial flexibility and may be one of the factors slowing down Bolt Food’s competitiveness in Portugal.

Precisely because of this tension, we’ve already taken the initiative to confirm with our external counsel (DLA Piper), who are handling the reclassification cases, whether we can safely reintroduce some types of communication (e.g. activation flows, educational messages) without undermining our position in ongoing litigation.


+*Recommended approach*+
DLA’s recommended approach regarding communications can be summed up like this:

* *Minimize direct communications with individual couriers.* The more Bolt communicates directly, especially with instructions, warnings, or performance-related messages, the stronger the evidence of control and disciplinary power → higher reclassification risk.
* *Prefer fleet-level communications.* Since fleets are the contractual counterpart in Portugal, communications should primarily go to them, not individual couriers. This helps maintain the legal separation.
* *If direct courier comms are unavoidable:*

      a) *Limit them strictly to platform integrity/safety issues* (e.g. fraud, food safety, thermal bag).

      b) *Keep messages neutral, factual, and T&Cs-based, without managerial tone, motivation, or coaching.*

      c) *Use in-app notifications* (linked to use of the app) rather than SMS/email, as these are harder to frame as    “management orders.”

* *Avoid “guidelines” or performance coaching.* Anything suggesting Bolt dictates how couriers dress, communicate, or organize work is seen as managerial authority and increases risk.
* *Blocking communications: safest to notify fleets only.* If couriers must be notified (DSA/PWD), keep it minimal and procedural, framed as transparency—not discipline.

*In short:* Communicate with fleets wherever possible, avoid “managing” couriers through comms, and if messages are necessary, keep them factual, limited, and in-app.


+*Conclusion*+

In summary, we are not being overly cautious—the legal and litigation risks in Portugal are real, as court cases demonstrate. That said, there is space to carefully reintroduce certain low-risk, neutral communications, provided they remain factual, limited, and avoid any appearance of managing couriers’ work. However, if the business decides to proceed with direct courier communications, we will of course provide guidance to minimise the risk as much as possible.

As [@lachlan.craig|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U03JV6YRREZ] is leaving us soon, I'm reaching out to you. Could you please tell me what were the reasons to not put the basis pass withdrawal (i have checked the apps and there's such option actually) into the T&Cs? I was testing the app and it seemed to be like that:
the customer books the e-scooter for upcoming 10 mins for XX EUR (this amount is charged at default once the customer confirms the booking). the customer can cancel the reservation for free within 10 mins, the whole amount is refunded within 14 days and no fees are charged provided that the customer hasn't used the charged amount at all. If the customer has used it but not used the whole charged fee and some amount remains, the difference is refunded within 14 days.are you able to confirm the basic pass process described as above too? thank you!

*Thiago Del Bel*  [11:00 AM|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/D09C51JP39R/p1756371635092039]

Hey [@jolanta.prystupa|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U093LU2PC3H], nice to e-meet you too

I wasn’t deeply involved in this initiative, but if I remember correctly the main reason is that passes are not exactly a subscription but rather a package of minutes the user can hire and use within a certain time threshold (e.g., 30 min in 24 hours). Thus, in theory, we are not really required to issue partial refunds to users. However, to avoid user friction and unnecessary scrutiny/disputes, we decided to allow users to cancel the pass and obtain a full or partial refund depending on whether the minutes have been used or not.

This approach was indeed inspired by the withdrawal right (proportional refund of the price of the services) but is not a perfect fit. Therefore, we avoided explicitly linking the cancellation option within the Bolt app to the EU withdrawal right in case, for instance, we decide to adopt a more aggressive approach in the future

.As for the reservation, that’s the default process at Bolt and many competitors. Reservation is free for X minutes and the actual price (passes or pay as you go) only gets charged after the free reservation period ends. Therefore, if user reserve the scooter and cancel it before the ride starts or the free reservation period ends, the ride is cancelled and nothing is charged. Anything that has been charged (pass price or pre-authorisation) is refunded/canceled.

I hope this helps

Hope you're all well.I wanted to bring to your attention — and formally close the loop on — a data handling issue from earlier this year that was already resolved at the time, but not shared with you then. We believe it’s important you are aware so similar issues don’t reoccur.

*What happened*
 In March 2025, a [+Google Sheet+|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1fQsJprJ68WAZPobCWLFhiLINIcmsSNbLsQnQPKHxD4g/edit?gid=0#gid=0] created by a member of your CS team in Egypt was inadvertently shared with “anyone with the link” access. The file contained driver-related information of approximately 10,000 drivers in Egypt and was flagged to us externally by a security researcher.

*Action taken immediately*
The file was swiftly restricted to not allow anyone with a link to access it, and no evidence of misuse was found.
We also analysed whether this breach would need to be notified to an Authority and concluded that it is not reportable as the supervisory authority under Egyptian law has not been operationalised yet, however, as our Partner, you should perform your own assessment.

*Why we’re sharing this now*
 While mitigation happened quickly, we realised recently that this had not been communicated to you. We want to ensure full transparency and make sure you’re aware, given the file originated from your CS operations.

*Recommendations*
 To help avoid a repeat, we recommend that your CS team:

* Revisit how Google Sheets are shared and ensure only _Bolt users_ have access. More documents with personal data, we'd recommend that you _restrict_ the file to be invite only.
* Remind your personnel of Bolt’s expectations on secure data handling and using Bolt-managed hardware/systems only.

Any questions, let me know.

Thank you.
{panel}

Hi team, 

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

*** Worth double-checking the purposes for keeping this data on the account - I assume it is primarily for safety, disputes and fraud. If so, and {color:#ff991f}*if the data being stored is enough to cover these*{color}, then this is fine.
