h1. Clarification

h2. 
Investigation

The root of the issue is in the way alters automation decomposes an alter to apply it on sharded schemas. While a full alter script produced by skeema is decomposed into 3 parts (logical schema name, table name and statement body - [https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/service/QueryHelper.ts#L40|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/service/QueryHelper.ts#L40]), a special case for table deletion is not covered.

A special case for table deletion is: a table is renamed into a table with a postfix containing a date and the {{_del}} postfix (see here: [https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/tooling_scripts/db/diff/alter-automation/compatibility.js#L49|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/tooling_scripts/db/diff/alter-automation/compatibility.js#L49]). Such tables are automatically deleted later by SREDB scripts.

With that, a rename statement will contain an actual sharded runtime schema to run on but a logical schema in the `rename` statement for both - ghost and native migration types (PRELIVE: [https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/stateMachine/processor/ConfirmSchemaDispatchStateProcessor.ts#L159|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/stateMachine/processor/ConfirmSchemaDispatchStateProcessor.ts#L159], [https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/stateMachine/processor/ConfirmSchemaDispatchStateProcessor.ts#L175|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/stateMachine/processor/ConfirmSchemaDispatchStateProcessor.ts#L175]. LIVE: [https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/stateMachine/processor/LiveInitSchemaMigrationStateProcessor.ts#L97|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/stateMachine/processor/LiveInitSchemaMigrationStateProcessor.ts#L97], [https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/stateMachine/processor/LiveInitSchemaMigrationStateProcessor.ts#L117|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/stateMachine/processor/LiveInitSchemaMigrationStateProcessor.ts#L117]).

h2. Proposed fix

There is no simple fix for this issue. We need to detect a {{rename alter}} statement and replace the target's logical schema with the runtime schema.

Possible solution is to update {{QueryHelper.composeRawStatement}} method ([https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/service/QueryHelper.ts#L103|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/service/QueryHelper.ts#L103]) for native applies and {{LiveInitStateProcessor}}'s process method ([https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/stateMachine/processor/LiveInitStateProcessor.ts#L48|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/stateMachine/processor/LiveInitStateProcessor.ts#L48]) to take into account `rename` statements.

I.e. to update {{statementParts.statement_body}} by replacing the logical schema with the runtime schema.

Probably it could be done by replacing the logical schema in {{QueryHelper.parseQuery}} ([https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/service/QueryHelper.ts#L40|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/foundation/backend/alter_orchestrator/main/service/QueryHelper.ts#L40]) with a placeholder and replacing it with a runtime schema in {{QueryHelper.composeRawStatement}} and {{LiveInitStateProcessor.process}}.

Benefit for the placeholder would be a guarantee for the correct schema, a rename alter to be executed on.

h2. Modification Plan

# Update {{QueryHelper.parseQuery}} to return {{statement_body}} with a runtime schema name placeholder;

# Update {{QueryHelper.composeRawStatement}} signature with an additional parameter for the runtime schema name and implementation to replace the abovementioned placeholder with the new parameter value;

# Use {{QueryHelper.composeRawStatement}} in {{LiveInitStateProcessor.process}}.

Specifically, infosec would only be approving VNGcloud for a single usecase “[Data Residency with Periodic Exports|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/x/b4KnfAE]”. The security requirements set in that document keep some separation between VNGCloud and Bolt Central AWS, and additionally ensure that only encrypted data is delivered to the server hosting provider. The keys are never stored in VNGCloud, so a server/infrastructure compromise would not lead to a data compromise.

This is why we haven’t set the same expectations as a “full cloud provider” - which would theoretically be allowed to host the entire Bolt production environment.

Summary:

* *Issue:* Hopp Driver based in Toronto, Canada, reports that his contact details were altered without his knowledge or consent.
* *Issue History:* 
** The driver reported the issue in early August 2025 across multiple Beehive support cases after noticing he couldn't sign in and his information was changed. He was unable to receive OTPs due to the changes. 
** Of note, the driver reached out to 1) [+info@gethopp.com+|mailto:info@gethopp.com] and then separately to 2) [+privacy@bolt.eu+|mailto:privacy@bolt.eu] to raise this issue, where he also included AKI Information in CC. 
** On the same day the requests were raised, Bolt CS restored the driver’s information and signed out all devices (the case handled via [+info@gethopp.com+|mailto:info@gethopp.com], not by the Privacy team)
** On 22 August 2025, AKI contacted [+privacy@bolt.eu+|mailto:privacy@bolt.eu] and asked us to confirm receipt, verify the circumstances, and report back on whether we’ve responded to the applicant by 15 Sept 2025.
* *Root Cause Investigation:* Engineers provided [+two possible explanations+|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02H52XUKPG/p1755868081312769] for the unauthorized changes, which were made on March 24, 2025. There are two suspicious logins:
** *Explanation 1:* The change was made by the "Driver" via the Driver Profile service, likely after the driver shared a 6-digit login code with an attacker.
** *Explanation 2:* Login occurred from a Windows desktop using a VPN IP address, and the password was changed from the same IP. The login involved a phone OTP, with no direct evidence of unauthorized access from this perspective.
* *Conclusion*: There's no definitive answer on whether the account owner or a malicious actor made the changes, but the latter is considered more likely. The issue was handled promptly by Hopp CS and the driver was back online quickly after raising the issue.

➡️ For a more detailed overview, see the fact-finding doc: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1qavO0cDljF1Rq5INwCyAIMhYgkFgndvLrY7B6F640So/edit?usp=sharing|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1qavO0cDljF1Rq5INwCyAIMhYgkFgndvLrY7B6F640So/edit?usp=sharing|smart-link]

* Explanation 1:

** Login most likely was performed 2 minutes prior to that via phone: 24 March 2025 at 12:04:27(UTC+02:00)
** Login via phone requires 6-digit code to be shared with attacker. Most likely code was shared by the driver, and this allowed attacker to log in.
* Explanation 2:
** Login was done from the Windows desktop computer
** He logged in from Windows 10 desktop on 24 March 2025, 10:04:27 GMT, from IP 146.70.198.19 (which is also from Canada), and his *password was changed* from the same IP.
** He logged in with the phone OTP. From what we see, there is no evidence of unauthorised access.
** All the driver logins you can see yourself in the "Refresh token" tab of the Driver profile in admin ([+link+|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet/drivers/edit/6899932?tab=refreshTokens&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A50%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn])
** However, this IP is used as a VPN [+https://www.criminalip.io/asset/report/146.70.198.19+|https://www.criminalip.io/asset/report/146.70.198.19]

*Questions have great clarity and are well structured:* This is the most critical area. Clear and well-structured questions lay the groundwork for meaningful user interviews and hence the quality of data collection. In order to achieve this, questions need to meet the following criteria:

* Clarity: Questions are direct, clear, easy to understand & relevant, avoiding ambiguity & complexity so that interviewees respond comfortably and accurately.
* Simple & easy to understand language
* Behavioural Relevance: Questions are rooted in actual behaviour/ experiences
* Well structured: Questions start easy and then move from broader topics to more specific ones



*Questions are neutral:* Maintaining neutrality ensures that participant responses reflect their true thoughts, feelings,and experiences without being influenced by the interviewer’s opinions, assumptions, or biases. Without neutrality, data integrity can be compromised. In order to achieve neutrality, questions need to meet the following criteria:

* Neutral Language: interviewer avoids using language that suggests a preferred response or judgement (no leading questions)
* Non-judgmental attitude
* Open-ended-questions encourage participants to speak freely without being led toward specific answers by the questions (no yes/no questions, or those which only allow for one answer)
* No assumptions: interviewer does not assume participant’s feelings or thoughts, instead they ask clarifying questions



*Each question has its probing and follow-up questions:* These questions enable the interviewer to ask follow-up or probing questions that encourage participants to elaborate on their responses, which is  important for gaining deeper insights. Probing and follow-up questions allow:

* Elaboration: interviewer asks questions that prompt participants to provide more detail, context, or examples
* Depth of inquiry: probing dives into feelings, motivations, underlying patterns --> more meaningful insights”

Hi Elīna,

Thank you for the detailed clarification. Let me provide further context and address the points you raised:

* *Type of Insurance*
You are correct that _Erhvervsansvarsforsikring_ (business liability insurance) is the Danish equivalent of commercial liability insurance. It protects companies against financial claims if their business activities cause injury, loss, or damage to people or property. This aligns with the requirement that all affiliated vehicles must hold valid commercial liability insurance.
* *Automatic Enrollment – Clarification*
The idea is *not* that FOs would be enrolled into a Bolt-provided insurance policy. Instead, in cases where it turns out that a vehicle is not insured (for example, if documentation is outdated or a policy has expired), the *insurance company would automatically enroll them into coverage*. This ensures that both Bolt and the FO remain compliant and protected.
** This enrollment would only happen if the FO is found to be uninsured.
** It would come with a *small fee charged directly by the insurance company*.
** I am happy to follow up with the insurance partner to obtain exact details of the fee structure.
* *Underlying Concern*
Our main concern is twofold:
*# Policies expiring without being renewed in time.
*# Cases where, despite document submission, the FO ends up not actually being covered (e.g., invalid policy).

This mechanism of automatic enrollment acts as a safeguard against these gaps, ensuring continuous coverage without putting Bolt in a position of breaching its legal obligation as the dispatch centre.

 _SELLING: Selling products containing cannabis or THC is strictly prohibited in Azerbaijan, regardless of the channel, method or format. Both substances are classified as narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances under national and international law. Their sale, distribution, and possession—even in small amounts—are criminal offenses that may result in imprisonment (3 to 7 years). The situation is different for CBD. While CBD is not explicitly banned or classified as a narcotic or psychotropic substance under Azerbaijani law, its sale is not clearly regulated either. This legal ambiguity means CBD products are not outright illegal, but they exist in a regulatory vacuum, with no clear framework for their classification, sale, or oversight. In case of wanting to proceed with CBD products, please consult legal team separately._
_There are no specific obligations or liabilities imposed on Bolt Food for enabling sales of CBD products by merchants or by Bolt Market itself. * _DISCOUNTING: Regarding CBD products then no specific provisions. Since the legal framework is absent, businesses act at their own risk and should monitor for future changes in regulation - please consult legal if interested to proceed with this. For THC and cannabis products - prohibbited since sale itself is prohibbited._ 
* _COMMUNICATION: For THC and cannabis - advertising and any comms are strictly prohibbited since sale itself if prohibbited. For CBD products: No specific advertising restrictions exist under current Azerbaijani law. However, the lack of regulation does not mean full legal certainty, and caution should be exercised in case new policies are introduced. Please consult legal separately if interested of proceeding with this._

Thanks a lot for sharing your view on this, Deborah — I really see the point you make about Bolt’s image and how we want to come across as fair and professional. I’m fully aligned on that.



Where I’d be more careful is with the idea of an apology. In Romanian law an apology in this context could be read as admitting liability, which would actually strengthen the partner’s case in court. Civil Code art. 1349 and 1357 on tort liability are clear here. That’s why my strong recommendation is to avoid apologizing. I dislike to reference my experience in Glovo again, but I have been in court with partners using appologies like this against Glovo. 



What we can safely do is keep the tone constructive, clarify things in a neutral way, and close the cooperation professionally — that protects Bolt’s reputation without creating legal risk.

Hi [~accountid:712020:e33d3b05-13ba-4374-b342-d0e2cc8272e7] - thank you for the request. Please find privacy’s analysis below:

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Conclusion:* the document is formally defective from privacy law perspective. However, mainly the risks sit with Citi, not Bolt. It would be low risk for Bolt to proceed as is.
{panel}

*Details of privacy's assessments & identified risks:*

The “Global KYC Data Sharing Consent Letter” provided by Citi is framed as a *consent form*, but its structure is unusual and legally unnecessary:
* *Consent is not required* for Citi’s KYC processing, as data collection is mandated under Taiwan’s AML/KYC legal framework.
* The format is problematic in that it requests *Bolt, as a legal entity*, to “consent” to processing of personal data belonging to specific individuals (e.g., Ahto Kink). Under Taiwan’s PDPA, only natural persons can consent to the processing of their personal data.
From a strict compliance perspective, the form does *not make sense* and would ideally need revision to align with lawful collection standards. However, given Citi’s regulatory obligations and the practical context, *I would consider risk exposure for Bolt as low, because:*
# There is a clear *regulatory basis* (KYC obligations) for the data collection.
# Liability for improperly framed consent rests primarily with Citi.
# The scope of *personal data* involved appears *minimal* (likely limited to Ahto as responsible person).
# The form is a *standard Citi template*, and re-negotiating would be time-consuming and likely very difficult, which would be impractical in this context.

# *Consent Not Required for In-App Banners*
In-app marketing banners are not subject to ePrivacy consent rules. As they do not constitute direct electronic communications (e.g., email, SMS), *soft opt-in requirements do not apply*. 
# *Use of Data Across Bolt Products – Legitimate Interest*
The key legal issue is whether Bolt can use personal data (including usage data) collected in connection with one Bolt product to promote another Bolt product. As all products are under the same controller and privacy notices generally state that user data may be used for marketing, *legitimate interest is likely a valid legal basis*.

However, *no formal Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA)* has yet been completed & prviacy notices would need to clearly state this is possible. *Clause 17 - Notices*
We’ve added email as a form of notice

Hi [~accountid:5ccfd257beee910dc4e37b1b] the agreement was signed on 19 September 2024.



{color:#0747a6}*_If we engage with a candidate they introduced to us and hire them in the end, do we have to pay them again for that candidate?_*{color}

*Yes*, Bolt will have to pay Triage a full fee *again* if it engages with a candidate introduced by Triage within a defined period.

This is confirmed in:

* *Clause 3.6 of the Terms of Business*:
“Should the Client subsequently re-engage the Candidate within a period of *12 calendar months from the date of Termination of the Engagement or withdrawal of the offer*, a *full Fee* will be payable with no entitlement to a refund.”
* *Clause 1.1.1 of the Fee Schedule* further supports this by stating a Fee is payable:
“If a Candidate commences an Engagement within 12 months of the later of:
(a) an Introduction;
(b) the Client’s first interview with the Candidate;
(c) the Client’s withdrawal of an offer of Engagement; or
(d) the Candidate’s earlier rejection of an offer…”

🔹 *Conclusion:* If the second candidate was introduced by Triage and Bolt now decides to engage them, *even after hiring and terminating a previous candidate*, Bolt will be liable for *a new fee*.


{color:#0747a6}*_I think it says the period is 12 months until we have to pay them if we reengage with an candidate, is the 12 months counted from when we signed the contract with them or is the 12 months starting when they introduce the candidate to us?_*{color}

The 12-month period is counted from when the candidate was introduced to Bolt, not from the date of contract signature.

This is established in:

* *Clause 1.1.1 of the Fee Schedule*:
“...within 12 months of *whichever is the later of*:
(a) an Introduction;
(b) the Client’s first interview with the Candidate;
(c) the Client’s withdrawal of an offer...”

🔹 *Conclusion:* The 12-month clock starts from *the later of the introduction date, interview date, or offer date*—not the date Bolt signed the engagement letter.


{color:#0747a6}*_Also, if it is written that we need to pay them a fee for this candidate that we would like to reengage with? How much is the fee?_*{color}

The applicable fee is *15% of the total gross compensation* for the candidate.

This is derived from:

* The *Confirmation of Instructions (COI)* (Page 3), under _Anticipated Fees_:
“*25% of total gross compensation*”
* However, *Clause 7.2.1* of the Terms was *varied in the COI to 15%*:
“Clause 7.2.1 is varied from 25% to *15%*.”
* Furthermore, *Clause 7.4* states:
“The Company will use the varied fee rate above for the purposes of calculating any charges and / or fees due under clause 7.2.”

🔹 *Conclusion:* Bolt will be required to pay *15% of the total gross compensation* (excluding equity and company car as per variations) if it re-engages the second candidate introduced by Triage.

If Triage is not successful in placing a candidate with Bolt, the outcome and Bolt’s obligations depend on how far the search progressed—as the fees are staged and non-refundable depending on how far the recruitment process progressed:

* *No shortlist submitted* → likely no fee, except possible expenses.
* *Shortlist submitted, but no hire* → *1/3 of the fee is payable*.
* *Candidate accepted offer, but didn’t join* → up to *full fee* may be due.

# Contractual Terms and Unilateral Changes

We acknowledge your readiness to allow Rimi a 90-day period to respond to proposed T&C updates, with non-response resulting in continuation under the previous terms. We confirm that this solution is legally sound and acceptable to Rimi, provided that:

* No changes come into force without signed Addendum.
* Non-response within the response period (30 or 90 days) will be treated as non-acceptance and the agreement continues under previous terms.
* The process is clearly defined in the contract to avoid ambiguity.

This approach ensures contractual continuity and protects both parties against unintended contractual amendments.

 

# Responsibility for Goods

We reconfirm Rimi’s position that:

* Our responsibility extends only to proper collection, packing, and marking of the goods. We do not accept responsibility for the delivery process or quality issues arising during delivery, as we have no contractual link with the courier.
* We reject the requirement to close bags, as this is not always feasible nor practiced in the market due to the nature of goods. Proper packaging and marking are sufficient to ensure traceability and order control.

We accept the wording proposed in your response, specifically:

_“Bolt shall be liable for any loss or damage to goods after handover from Rimi until delivery to the end customer, assuming Rimi i) collected order in the timely manner; ii) order is correctly collected & packed; iii) order is correctly marked for Delivery Partners’ collection.”_

Please ensure this wording is reflected in the Special Terms.

 

# Customer Issue Resolution and Deductions

We appreciate the clarification on refund management and accept the suggested structure with the following adjustments:

* Refund reporting will be weekly, with a 30-day window for Rimi to approve or dispute specific cases via the portal.
* Real-time intervention is not required, avoiding overloading store personnel or call centers.
* Rimi will handle investigation internally (with use of system data and security footage where applicable), and no involvement of store staff or call center will be necessary.

This solution balances operational practicality with financial transparency and is aligned with Rimi’s internal structure.

 

# Alcohol Sales and Legal Compliance

While we appreciate Bolt’s zero-tolerance approach and app-level compliance tools, we cannot accept liability caps that expose Rimi to regulatory risks (including license loss).

Therefore:

 The agreement must clearly state that at the point of delivery Bolt has obligation to:

# ensure that delivery of alcohol is conducted only during permitted alcohol sales hours. If order pick-up is conducted 1 hour before the permitted alcohol sales hours end, order delivery much be finished before the restriction is applicable;
# conduct and ensure proper age verification from ID;
# ensure that alcohol products are not handed to drunk persons.

If Bolt fails to ensure these requirements there might not be any hard monetary caps (e.g., EUR 50,000) for alcohol-related liabilities. This is non-negotiable due to the potential magnitude of risk to our alcohol license and business continuity as for violation of these requirements not only fines might be applicable, but there is a risk to loose alcohol sales license. We propose unlimited liability in case of license loss due to proven courier non-compliance

h3. *Key risk areas*

h4. 1. *Sub-processing restrictions (Clause 11)*

* Göteborgs Stad reserves the right to object to any new sub-processors within 30 days.
* Even transport sub-contractors are treated as sub-processors.
** We will need to sign separate agreements with these drivers/fleets. At the moment, we do not have such agreements in place as the usual position we maintain is that drivers/fleets are not our sub-processors.
* Risk: Operational disruption if any sub-processor (e.g., vehicle subcontractor or tech vendor) is rejected. In other words, this means that they need to confirm all of our suppliers (from infrastructure to marketing/analytics tools) IF any passenger data is included there.

h4. 2. *International transfers prohibited (Clause 12)*

* All personal data processing must remain within the EU/EEA unless specifically approved in writing.
* This includes technical processing, backups, or support.
* We have a number of tools that are US-hosted, including Google, AWS, Marketing, Analytics tools - we need to understand if these passengers will be treated as usual Bolt passengers or if we can restrict the use of some tools for this tender.

h4. 3. *Sensitive personal data in scope (Annex 1)*

* Agreement includes health-related travel data (disability, assistive needs), triggering Article 9 GDPR.
* Sensitive data must be handled with elevated safeguards and explicit consent.
* We will need to perform a separate assessment to document this data use + understand how practically we will receive/use this data.

h4. 4. *Detailed security requirements (Annex 1)*

* Lists specific technical and organizational measures (encryption, access logging, cryptographic protections, access segregation).
* Failure to meet any security standard may constitute a breach.
* InfoSec needs to validate existing measures against the listed requirements to see if we comply.

h4. 5. *Strict audit and access rights (Clause 8)*

* Municipality can audit Bolt’s premises, systems, and personnel without cause.
* Annual self-audit reporting also required.
* Infosec needs to be contacted regarding self-audit and what kind of annual audit reports we maintain.

h4. 6. *Data deletion and return obligations (Clause 16)*

* Processor must return or delete all data (including logs and metadata) within 30 days of contract end.
* At the moment, as far as I know, this is not feasible. There needs to be a discussion with product/engineering on how to ensure such deletion.



*Overall -* nothing out of ordinary, and we can proceed provided that we will be able to operationally comply with the requirements of the tender, including sub-contracting, data transfers, data deletion, and infosec requirements.

[~accountid:712020:d008dcec-6cfe-47e4-83a0-c29522744742] I did some researches.

In France, the legal requirement for taxis is to hold *assurance automobile à titre onéreux*. This is a specific form of car insurance that covers both the *vehicle* and the *driver’s professional liability* when carrying passengers for payment. Article R. 211-15 of the Code des assurances requires that the insurance certificate explicitly state when a vehicle is used for paid passenger transport, and Article R. 3120-4 of the Code des transports requires drivers to be able to present this justificatif d’assurance à titre onéreux at any time during checks. Because this policy already includes the professional liability element, a separate RC Pro (Responsabilité Civile Professionnelle) is not legally necessary for taxi activity: the “à titre onéreux” insurance alone satisfies the legal requirement. This is why insurers often sell “taxi packages” that combine both coverages in one contract.

For Bolt as a centrale de réservation, the obligation is to collect and verify this insurance certificate, alongside the other standard documents (driving licence, professional taxi card, ADS, and vehicle registration). The question of whose name the policy is in depends on the driver’s professional status. If the taxi is operated by an *independent ADS holder* (an owner-driver), it is entirely normal and compliant that the insurance is in the driver’s own name. If the taxi is operated under a *company ADS with employed drivers*, then the company should generally be the policyholder, since it holds the operating authorisation. In both cases, however, the decisive factor is not the name on the policy but whether the *vehicle and the activity of carrying paying passengers are clearly insured “à titre onéreux”*.

Therefore, for Bolt’s purposes, it is acceptable to collect and rely on these “taxi package” insurances, even when they are issued in the driver’s name, as long as they explicitly mention *à titre onéreux* and cover the vehicle used on the platform. A separate RC Pro certificate should not be required, since the assurance à titre onéreux already provides that protection.

*Employment & Driver Compliance Requirements – Tender Review Overview*

* +Employment Conditions & Collective Agreements+
** All drivers must be employed under terms equivalent to the Taxi Agreement, covering pensions and insurances (e.g., AGS, TFA, TGL), regardless of whether the operating company is formally bound by a collective bargaining agreement.
** *Obligations:*
*** Operators must document the suitability of each driver according to the prescribed profile.
*** Records must be retained for at least 12 months from the date of employment (or until the contract ends).
*** Background checks (criminal record extracts, references from former employers) are mandatory before employment.
*** Every driver must hold a *written employment contract*.
* +Driver Requirements & Service Standards+
** Drivers must meet extensive conduct, service, and operational requirements, including:
*** Daily license checks, uniforms, name/certification badges.
*** Knowledge of routes, strict service behavior rules, and complaint handling.
*** Restrictions on perfume use, phone conversations, and personal conduct.
*** Obligation to apologize on behalf of the authority if arriving late. 
* +Training & Certification Burden+
** A multi-step qualification system applies to all drivers:
*** Initial training, national certification, Swedish language testing (minimum B1), CPR/AED training, eco-driving, and customer service training.
*** Ongoing retraining and re-certification are mandatory.
*** Strict deadlines apply (3–6 months from first assignment).
*** Failure leads to immediate loss of driver authorization and potential financial penalties.
* +First Driver (“Försteförare”) Requirement+
** Operators with 10+ vehicles must appoint one or more “first drivers,” acting as quality ambassadors and trainers.
** *Obligations:*
*** Hold the highest driver authorization level.
*** Participate in city-led activities.
*** Receive a mandatory gross salary supplement of SEK 5,000/month.
* Employer Responsibility: The traffic company (main supplier as well as subcontractors) must ensure that:
** All work is carried out in line with laws, regulations, authority decisions, operational rules, and industry standards aimed at maintaining safety and reliability.
** All staff working with service journeys are familiar with the agreement and its contents.
** Drivers are immediately prevented from carrying out assignments under the agreement if the client revokes their authorization or if they no longer meet contractual conditions.
* *Risks*
** Since Bolt does not employ drivers directly, compliance depends entirely on FOs. However, the tender assigns accountability to the main contractor (us), creating *reclassification risk*: we are effectively mandating employment terms.
** Extensive control over driver behavior, service standards, and mandatory roles (e.g., “first driver” salary supplements) mirror *employer-style obligations*, reinforcing reclassification exposure.
** Even though enforcement sits with FOs, the main contractor could ultimately retain *legal and financial accountability*.
* *Operational Burden*
** Authorities may demand proof of compliance down to the individual level (e.g., payslips, pension deposits, insurance contributions).
** Monitoring, enforcing, and documenting compliance across a distributed driver base is *highly resource-intensive*, requiring continuous infrastructure.
** Coordinating and financing multi-step training, certification, and re-certification adds significant cost and complexity.
** Tracking compliance at scale demands advanced systems and back-office resources, with indirect financial exposure falling back on the operator (and, by extension, Bolt through accountability).

h3. *Subcontractors, Quality Controls, Complaints & Penalties*

* Using subcontractors: 
** The traffic company (includes both main supplier and subcontractors) is responsible for ensuring that any subcontractor meets the same requirements imposed on the operator itself, both regarding personnel and work. *The main supplier is liable for the subcontractor’s compliance as if it were its own*. The operator must coordinate and provide all requirements set by the client to the subcontractor and, upon request, present evidence showing that the subcontractor fulfills these requirements. 
** *A subcontractor may not engage its own subcontractors.* 
* Complaint handling is highly regulated: every complaint must be answered within 7 days, using a standard template. Delays = fines (2,500–5,000 SEK).
* Operators must maintain complaint ratios below 0.15%. Higher ratios trigger mandatory action plans, and after six months of high levels, the authority can cut assignments.

h3. *Sanctions, Unlimited Liability, Insurance* 

* Extensive penalty regime, with fines for administrative misses (late lists, missing documentation, non-compliance with subcontractor approval) and for service failures (late arrivals, driver misconduct, smoking in vehicles, wrong equipment, etc.).
* Standard fine: 10,000 SEK per breach, but many other specific fines range 500–20,000 SEK.
* Liability clauses impose broad responsibility for damages caused by the company, employees, or subcontractors ({color:#bf2600}or employees of subcontractors){color}. There is *no financial cap* beyond exclusion of indirect damages.
** Therefore - an extensive insurance should be in place for this tender - to be discussed with the Insurance Team. 
* *Risk:* Exposure to significant financial penalties, especially given the administrative intensity and the reliance on subcontracted drivers.

✅ *In conclusion:* This tender imposes *extensive employer-style obligations*, creating a high *reclassification risk*. It also generates a very *administration-heavy compliance burden*, especially around subcontractor control, driver training/certification, complaint handling, and reporting. The combination of unlimited liability, high penalties, and strict behavioral control of drivers makes this contract  *risky and costly* without investment in compliance infrastructure and legal safeguards (such as back-to-back protection in our subcontracting agreements and sufficient insurance).

Hey everyone, 
Sorry for late reply, 

Few separate issues here. 
The charge on the account that is from a user that reports has not used the service and is not on the platform (once confirmed with the user) should be blocked. In a case of unknown charges Bolt has nothing to do with the account and personal data breach. Even the block itself is not a definitive solution, as the fraudster (or in many case just a family member) in possession of the card can just make a new account. 

The charges, whether on an account with user not on a platform, or a user that is active on Bolt but has unknown charges are a Fraud issue. Refunds to these charges we do not do. And as per the current articles we '*advise them to contact their bank'.* The bank has additional information on verification upon authorization on charge and can determine how to proceed with the case. It is the proper flow, as if a true card abuse has happened, blocking the card in the bank is the number one step a user should take to prevent further charges. 
For recovery of funds, the proper solution is chargeback. We tend not to direct them towards that, in cases of friendly fraud or of abuse of this process, but directing them to the bank is sufficient as the bank knows the next steps and can determine whether it has the ability to submit the chargeback or not. 

For sharing info with the user, on the trip or the profile that is created, i would be very careful, data being sent openly. If it is received by authorities and approved by DPO office then data can be extracted and if we receive a chargeback in that flow we send information to the bank (automated process in most markets, Canada is still work in progress though). 

Let me know if there are any more questions,

*Additonal context:* 
We are preparing to trial *Notion* as a potential replacement for Confluence and as a consolidated productivity hub. The goal is to address long-standing challenges with knowledge management, while also introducing integrated AI capabilities that reduce tool fragmentation across the company.

Today, our documentation is spread across Confluence, Google Drive, Slack, Jira, GitHub, and Figma, which creates silos and makes it difficult to maintain accurate, reliable, and discoverable knowledge. Confluence adoption has been low due to poor UX, lack of integration with our daily workflows, and outdated content. At the same time, emerging AI use cases such as enterprise search, meeting transcription, and intelligent note-taking are currently only available in standalone tools, which risks adding even more fragmentation.

By trialing Notion, we aim to evaluate whether it can serve as a *centralized, all-in-one platform* for documentation, collaboration, and AI-powered productivity. This includes testing critical use cases such as:

* Centralized and always up-to-date documentation.
* Seamless integration with Google Workspace, Jira, and other core tools.
* AI-powered enterprise search, meeting transcription, and summarization.

Hi [~accountid:712020:db41f6cc-b777-4b3f-961b-09bab7b9da50],

In France, the legal requirement for taxis is to hold *assurance automobile à titre onéreux*. This is a specific form of car insurance that covers both the *vehicle* and the *driver’s professional liability* when carrying passengers for payment. Article R. 211-15 of the Code des assurances requires that the insurance certificate explicitly state when a vehicle is used for paid passenger transport, and Article R. 3120-4 of the Code des transports requires drivers to be able to present this justificatif d’assurance à titre onéreux at any time during checks. Because this policy already includes the professional liability element, a separate RC Pro (Responsabilité Civile Professionnelle) is not legally necessary for taxi activity: the “à titre onéreux” insurance alone satisfies the legal requirement. This is why insurers often sell “taxi packages” that combine both coverages in one contract.

For Bolt as a centrale de réservation, the obligation is to collect and verify this insurance certificate, alongside the other standard documents (driving licence, professional taxi card, ADS, and vehicle registration). The question of whose name the policy is in depends on the driver’s professional status. If the taxi is operated by an *independent ADS holder* (an owner-driver), it is entirely normal and compliant that the insurance is in the driver’s own name. If the taxi is operated under a *company ADS with employed drivers*, then the company should generally be the policyholder, since it holds the operating authorisation. In both cases, however, the decisive factor is not the name on the policy but whether the *vehicle and the activity of carrying paying passengers are clearly insured “à titre onéreux”*.

Therefore, for Bolt’s purposes, it is acceptable to collect and rely on these “taxi package” insurances, even when they are issued in the driver’s name, as long as they explicitly mention *à titre onéreux* and cover the vehicle used on the platform. A separate RC Pro certificate should not be required, since the assurance à titre onéreux already provides that protection. If the driver does not dispose of this “taxi package” insurance, we should be asking for both the RC Pro certificate and the insurance certificate. 

Happy to discuss this further, please let us know if you have any questions.

Hi [~accountid:712020:db41f6cc-b777-4b3f-961b-09bab7b9da50], 

The taxi fares in France are regulated in the annex of the [Arrêté du 22 janvier 2024 relatif aux tarifs des courses de taxi|https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/id/JORFTEXT000049040513], as amended in 2025. These regulations strictly govern taxi fares and determine how the taximeter must calculate the fare.

From a platform perspective, our objective is consumer transparency: we aim to provide passengers with an accurate price estimate of what the final fare will be as indicated by the taximeter. The price displayed in the app is therefore indicative only and not the final amount payable, as the regulated taximeter calculation prevails.

It is acceptable for Bolt to adjust tariff components (e.g. per-minute or per-km values) in our internal calculation model if this helps generate more accurate estimates. However, these adjusted components must never be shown to consumers as if they were the official regulated tariff structure.

*Conclusion:* It would not constitute a misleading practice to adjust the minimum per-minute value used in our calculation model, provided that this adjustment is solely for estimation purposes and to increase accuracy.

*Recommendation:* The description shown to consumers must remain fully consistent with the regulation and transparent as to the fact that the taximeter ultimately determines the price to be paid. 

Happy to discuss this further, please let us know if you have any further questions. 

Thank you !

# What is the legal entity “tree” or structure of Bolt Market and for Bolt Micromobility?
## The exact shareholding structure is available here: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/3169059494/Bolt+Subsidiaries+and+Partners|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/3169059494/Bolt+Subsidiaries+and+Partners|smart-link]  . As you can see, the ultimate parent company is Bolt Technology OÜ. Two direct subsidiaries Bolt Holdings OÜ and Bolt Operations OÜ hold the shares of all other local subsidiaries. 
## However, the entity tree structure does not reflect the Bolt Market / MM split. That means a local entity (e.g. SIA Bolt LV) can be the legal entity for local rides operations, Bolt Food, Bolt Market and MM. The only exception seems to be Bolt Store EE OÜ, which is a legal entity only dealing with Bolt Market. HEre’s the overview: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PAR/pages/5324276294/Legal+Entity+Logic|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PAR/pages/5324276294/Legal+Entity+Logic|smart-link] 
## I assume you are asking in relation to the SME definition. Only the finance team probably has the number necessary to determine that - but at first glance, I think  Bolt Store EE OÜ is the only one to possibly qualify as an SME; as all other entities operate several different business lines, thus their turnover / headcount exceeds the limits. 
# Does every legal entity need to report separately, or can we do a consolidated report? Could you refer to the place in the legislation that explains it? 
## As far as I can see, no legal entity level data is needed. Article 12(3) allows us to report on a “summary” / “conclusions” level - let’s interpret that in our favour. 



One more thought (probably not new info to you 😄 ) - Bolt Market does not import outside of EU. So even if we have the obligations of an operator (as non-SME trader), then probably the easiest approach from an operational side it to fully rely on upstream DDS when supplying the products in scope.

For completeness, I include my thoughts below on the main risks. This includes a *suggestion relating to the wording we can use when reaching out to the winner*s (see Point 1).

*Main Privacy Points To Note*

*(1) Requesting data from the winners*
* Technically, collecting a winner’s data for the purpose of sending them Bolt credits is not explicitly covered in our driver privacy notice. Although this is overall low risk, there is a still a transparency gap here, as driver’s may want to know why we need this information / submit requests to Bolt for the same.
* Ideally, when we reach out to the driver to request their account ID, name and email, {color:#4c9aff}*it would be helpful to include the following text in the message* {color}(if there is still time to do so): “_We will use this information to identify your Bolt account and to send you the Bolt credits. For further information on how we process your personal data, please check our_ [_privacy notice_|https://bolt.eu/sv-se/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/?category=rides]_._” 
** If this is not operationally possible at this stage then it is not a deal-breaker, but I am flagging just in case.
*(2) Encouraging drivers to download the Adventure Lab app*
* Technically, we require the *consent* of Bolt drivers to send them direct promotional comms about products provided by third parties (which would including certain comms encouraging drivers to download the Adventure Lab app). We therefore need to ensure that we are sending relevant comms only to drivers that have properly consented.
** In particular, we should only be sending *emails* and *push notifications* about Adventure Lab to drivers that have consented to ‘Partner Offers’ on their Bolt profile (*_this should already be the case_*, but flagging just in case this has been missed). Other promotion mediums (e.g., the landing page, OOH marketing) will not require driver consent.
* We should also ensure that the drivers are given the opportunity to *opt-out* of these promotional comms every time that they are sent (e.g., through an ‘unsubscribe’ link) - again, *_this should already be the case_*, but flagging just in case. I also note that in Finland 🇫🇮 the Finnish Direct Marketing Association maintains an email opt-out list (called the ‘Robinson List’) - before sending promotional emails to Finnish drivers, *was this list checked* to find those who have specified they do not want to receive such emails? (?) 
** If it wasn’t then I assume it is too late to do so, in which case I am flagging for completeness. 

Going forward, please ensure that any questions raised by the Privacy Team are answered before going ahead with the initiative, to avoid any operational friction further down the road 🙏  If you have any questions then let me know 🙂

* Bolt Club was set up to mirror Uber rewards program in Germany to lock-in scarce high-quality supply due to regulatory changes
* Bolt Club offers drivers different tiers (Gold, Platinum, Diamond) of rewards based on Fleet performance
* Rewards consist of third party offers (Fuel discounts, Car wash...), additional system functionality (SR, shorter order request distance...) and fixed fee bonuses
** Drivers receive weekly fixed fee bonus depeding on their activity and fleet tier. These bonuses on the higher end can equal to 15% kickback
** To balance this out Bolt increased their commision to 30% in DE.
** Fixed fees are payed out as normal supply campaigns
* There were no legal or regulatory hurdles
* This model works best in high demand areas with low supply ( Berlin is around 85% utilization) where drivers don't have to multiapp thus you have to lock them in
* Germany doesn't have any additional supply campaigns. Bolt Club supply spend is around 8% of GMV

Some Guidance:

*Monetary Limits:* It deals with claims less than KES 1million. 

*Time*: 60 days for hearing and resolution. In practice this doesn’t happen and typically it takes longer than 60 days for final judgment. 

*Representation*: Parties can go themselves and do not need lawyers to represent them and the hearings are held virtually. 

*Filing process*: There is a template form for the complaint and a template form for response. If the parties agree-they can ask the adjudicator to rule based on the written arguments rather than have to appear before. You can also just serve the claim via Whatsapp, SMS , e-mail. 

*Link:* [https://judiciary.go.ke/small-claims-court/|https://judiciary.go.ke/small-claims-court/|smart-link] 

*Advice:* It works fairly well for debt collection in terms of time because a decision is given faster than in court. Typically once you file, you get a hearing date within 2 weeks . *The issue is enforcement;* if you had judgment in your favour, then you have to apply for warrants of arrest, or get an auctioneer to attach the assets of the debtor. *Consider that (1) we don’t have courier’s physical addresses-it will be difficult to trace them to even collect the payment (2) you are unlikely in most cases to even find that the courier has assets that can be sold to recover the debt .*

If you want to still want to pursue this then my suggestion is this:

# Set the threshold for follow up on payment- it may not be worth following up payment of small amounts.
# Send a demand in app/via SMS/e-mail about the payment due to us. 
# You can then pursue the couriers who have responded to our demand and (1) discuss a payment plan with them or (2) pursue the claim in small claims court.
# If the number of couriers you want to pursue in court are many, then you can engage a lawyer to help with the process *BUT LEGAL FEES WILL BE A BOLT FOOD COST NOT LEGAL TEAM COST.*

Hi [~accountid:712020:6cf755e4-2536-45f4-814b-7e7ef0cdbd97] !

Thanks for raising this – it’s an important point as courier engagement and reclassification risks need to be carefully balanced in Portugal.


+*Where our risk lies*+
The main legal risk is reclassification of couriers as employees. Portuguese courts have been increasingly sensitive to this, particularly in the food delivery space, and we’ve already seen precedents where factors such as control over couriers (instructions, mandatory shifts, monitoring, penalties, and training) were decisive for reclassification.

Any direct or prescriptive communication to couriers that could be interpreted as Bolt “managing” or “supervising” their work (e.g. telling them when, how or where to work, or disciplining them) increases exposure.


+*How big the risk is*+
In Portugal, the risk is very high compared to other EU markets because:

* The Labour Inspectorate and courts are active in pursuing reclassification in the sector. 
* Bolt itself has 46 cases on record: Bolt was absolved in 34 (but 6 of them have been appealed); and 11 remain pending a first instance decision.
* Independent couriers were phased out in April 2023, with fleets now supplying labour. Even so, aggressive comms to couriers can still be cited as evidence of hidden employment relationships.
* Litigation costs, potential back-pay of employment benefits, and reputational risks make this a top legal exposure for Delivery.
* The indicative cost exposure per reclassification case is in average € 101,503.01 or € 93,512.18 (depending on the start date of the calculation - meaning, if reference date is the creation of the account or the date of the inspection).


+*Market intelligence / what competitors are doing*+
We don’t have clear evidence that competitors in PT have completely frozen comms. However, we know competitors are losing some of the reclassification cases in Portugal that they are part of, while Bolt has so far avoided such outcomes. This reinforces that our more conservative strategy has been paying off from a litigation-risk perspective.


+*Sensitivity to business impact*+
We are very conscious that this cautious approach restricts some commercial flexibility and may be one of the factors slowing down Bolt Food’s competitiveness in Portugal.

Precisely because of this tension, we’ve already taken the initiative to confirm with our external counsel (DLA Piper), who are handling the reclassification cases, whether we can safely reintroduce some types of communication (e.g. activation flows, educational messages) without undermining our position in ongoing litigation.



+*Recommended approach*+
DLA’s recommended approach regarding communications can be summed up like this:

* *Minimize direct communications with individual couriers.* The more Bolt communicates directly, especially with instructions, warnings, or performance-related messages, the stronger the evidence of control and disciplinary power → higher reclassification risk.
* *Prefer fleet-level communications.* Since fleets are the contractual counterpart in Portugal, communications should primarily go to them, not individual couriers. This helps maintain the legal separation.
* *If direct courier comms are unavoidable:*

      a) *Limit them strictly to platform integrity/safety issues* (e.g. fraud, food safety, thermal bag).

      b) *Keep messages neutral, factual, and T&Cs-based, without managerial tone, motivation, or coaching.*

      c) *Use in-app notifications* (linked to use of the app) rather than SMS/email, as these are harder to frame as  “management orders” and are also less tangible evidence in court proceedings.

* *Avoid “guidelines” or performance coaching.* Anything suggesting Bolt dictates how couriers dress, communicate, or organize work is seen as managerial authority and increases risk.
* *Blocking communications: safest to notify fleets only.* If couriers must be notified (DSA/PWD), keep it minimal and procedural, framed as transparency—not discipline.

*In short:* Communicate with fleets wherever possible, avoid “managing” couriers through comms, and if messages are necessary, keep them factual, limited, and in-app.



+*Conclusion*+

In summary, we are not being overly cautious—the legal and litigation risks in Portugal are real, as court cases demonstrate. That said, there is space to carefully reintroduce certain low-risk, neutral communications, provided they remain factual, limited, and avoid any appearance of managing couriers’ work. 

If the business decides to proceed with direct courier communications, we will, of course, provide guidance to minimise the risk as much as possible; but will also need to inform our external counsel (DLA), as well as the Bolt employees who act as witnesses in court (David and Barbara), so they are fully aware of any operational changes and can continue defending us effectively in ongoing proceedings.

so i have added driver/rider quartiles. We’re calculating quartiles based on the total number of CS tickets each driver raises in their city (from first ride onward). Drivers/riders are ranked by ticket volume and split into Q1–Q4:

* Q1 (light raisers) = bottom 25% (e.g. 0–1 tickets)
* Q4 (heavy raisers) = top 25% (e.g. 7+ tickets)

Quartiles are assigned once per driver/rider–city based on their total tickets (lifetime-to-date), so the label (Q1–Q4) stays fixed. The evaluation month filter (e.g. 6m) simply restricts the view to drivers who have been on the platform at least that long; it doesn’t recalculate quartiles at month 6.
Example:

* Driver A → 2 tickets → Q1, active 12m → included in 6m evaluation.
* Driver B → 10 tickets → Q4, active 4m → excluded in 6m evaluation.

So when you filter for 6,12,24m evaluation, you’ll only see drivers who reached 6,12,24 months, with their original quartile labels.

Here is a short manual how to proceed



# *Attach new volume*

* Attach a new EBS volume (e.g., {{nvme2}}) same size and tags

# *Format and mount*

{noformat}mkfs.xfs /dev/nvme2n1
mkdir -p /mnt/backup
mount /dev/nvme2n1 /mnt/backup
{noformat}

# *Stop MySQL*

{noformat}systemctl stop mysqld
# or
systemctl stop mysql
{noformat}

# *Copy data*


Use {{rsync}} to preserve permissions, symlinks, hardlinks, and attributes:

{noformat}rsync -aHAX --progress /mysql/ /mnt/backup/
{noformat}

# *Verify copy*

* Compare sizes:
{noformat}du -sh /mysql
du -sh /mnt/backup
{noformat}
* Optionally check file counts:
{noformat}find /mysql | wc -l
find /mnt/backup | wc -l
{noformat}

# *Remount*

* Rename old directory (backup):
{noformat}mv /mysql /mysql.old
mkdir /mysql
{noformat}
* Unmount temporary mount and remount permanently:
{noformat}umount /mnt/backup
mount /dev/nvme2n1 /mysql
{noformat}
* Update {{/etc/fstab}} for persistence:
{noformat}echo "/dev/nvme2n1 /mysql xfs defaults 0 0" >> /etc/fstab
{noformat}

# *Start MySQL*

{noformat}systemctl start mysqld
{noformat}

# *Validate*

* Check logs to confirm MySQL starts without errors.
* Verify data is intact and queries work.

# *Cleanup*

* Once confirmed stable, remove {{/mysql.old}} and  detach/remove the old LVM volume.
